value.text: The deadly shooting of a 30-year-old Army veteran by Palm Beach County sheriff's deputies near Boca Raton is raising familiar questions about how law enforcement officers respond to armed people experiencing a mental health crisis. WPTV's Michael Hoffman sat down with a former federal law enforcement officer and trainer to examine how officers are taught to de-escalate crises and how those encounters can become life-or-death situations.The shooting happened Wednesday night at Sandalfoot Square after deputies responded to a call involving Joshua Senfeld, an Army veteran who Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said was armed and threatening suicide. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said deputies spent more than an hour trying to resolve the encounter peacefully before Senfeld brandished a firearm in their direction and deputies opened fire. Senfeld died at the scene.The incident is under investigation. The deputies involved were placed on administrative leave, and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, Palm Beach County State Attorney's Office and PBSO's Violent Crimes Division are investigating. Bradshaw said Senfeld's family contacted authorities and that Senfeld was suicidal and armed. The sheriff said Senfeld was an Army veteran who authorities understood had post-traumatic stress disorder."He was very suicidal and was armed," Bradshaw said.Bradshaw said deputies negotiated with Senfeld for more than 90 minutes. During that time, one deputy who is also a veteran tried to connect with him."They talked to this guy a long, long time trying to talk him down," Bradshaw said. "Even one of our guys who's a vet kind of connected with him a little bit and told him, 'Hey, you know, we're going to get you the help you need.'"Bradshaw said Senfeld eventually became agitated and began standing with his firearm in what the sheriff described as a "ready position." PBSO said Senfeld brandished the gun in the direction of deputies before they fired. To better understand how officers are trained to handle situations like these, Hoffman sat down with Tim Miller of Lion Heart Protection Strategies.Miller, a former Secret Service agent, former federal law enforcement officer and law enforcement trainer, told Hoffman that Crisis Intervention Training is one way officers are taught to respond to people experiencing crises."There's a program called Crisis Intervention Training where officers are trained specifically for this kind of thing," Miller said.Miller said the training can involve mental health professionals teaching law enforcement officers techniques designed to help them communicate with people during a crisis."We were trained by some of the best psychiatrists, psychologists," Miller told Hoffman. "They're not police training police in many cases. These are professional mental health experts, training officers on how to connect, how to dissuade, how to hear things with the way the person's speaking, to try to understand for exactly the purposes of de-escalating so that everyone goes home safe."Miller, who is also a Marine Corps veteran, pointed to veteran suicide as another part of the tragedy surrounding the encounter.The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs' 2024 National Veteran Suicide Prevention Annual Report found there were 6,407 veteran suicides in 2022, an average of 17.6 per day. Those were the most recent figures available in that edition of the VA's annual report.Miller also spoke about the lasting impact a deadly encounter can have on the officers involved."Whoever had to take that shot is going to have to deal with that the rest of his life, even though he or she didn't have a choice," Miller told Hoffman. "They're going to have to live with that. And that's an unfortunate additional tragedy."The circumstances of Wednesday's shooting remain under investigation, meaning the findings of investigators, rather than the broader training principles discussed by Miller, will ultimately determine what happened during the encounter.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Jupiter council members discussed the future of a prime piece of town waterfront in a special town council meeting Thursday evening.In the hours-long meeting, town leaders heard from a developer proposing 44 condos and a 110-room hotel, along with a restaurant and a marina that would take up about 4.5 acres of the 10.5-acre site.WATCH: Jupiter council heard a developer's plan for the former Suni Sands waterfront siteThe site was once home to the Suni Sands Mobile Home Park off A1A. Development plans stalled after the discovery of Native American archaeological sites, but the town and the developer came to an agreement earlier this year to allow development on part of the parcel, with the town purchasing just over an acre of the waterfront for $10 million.The developer is asking the town for a number of waivers in its plan. He told the council Thursday he's looking to make the space a place the community can enjoy while preserving much of the land."We still wanted to work with the town and create something that we could build there that would be something I would be as proud of as I have been with Love Street," Sperry Parcel Developer Charles Modica said.Dozens of people turned up for the evening meeting to voice concerns over developing one of the town's last waterfront sites."Suni Sands is more than a piece of property. It's part of the natural legacy of our community and once it's developed, we can't get it back. Some things are too valuable to replace," a young resident opposed to the project said.Thursday's special meeting was the first reading of the proposed rule changes that could allow the development.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Ohio governor candidate Vivek Ramaswamy's controversial attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, is off the air after the Republican spent about a quarter of what his campaign initially said it would invest to run it.Ramaswamy said during a campaign appearance in Vandalia, Ohio, on Thursday that the ad’s planned run was over. His campaign originally said it would spend $4 million to air the ad, but data from the ad-tracking firm AdImpact showed it spent roughly $1 million.RELATED STORY | Trump in Ohio and Obama in Georgia make closing stretch appeals to midterm voters in pivotal statesThe divisive spot had provoked backlash in Ohio and among politicians of both parties across the nation. It featured Donna Arthur calling her daughter a lifelong liar. That was despite the two having not seen each other for nearly 50 years. Arthur lost custody of her children in 1978 after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12.Ramaswamy had defended the ad, though a later version trimmed some portions.President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance said they supported the decision to air the ad. The president said he told Ramaswamy to leave it on the air, adding “she's fair game.”Ohio governors past and present, alumni of Ramaswamy’s Catholic high school in Cincinnati and others had urged him to pull it down.RELATED STORY | Trump strongly defends controversial Ramaswamy ad featuring opponent's motherActon’s campaign said the ad was “despicable” and should never have run and that Ramaswamy should have apologized.

An 18-month seawall replacement project on Palm Beach is raising questions from residents and beachgoers about why the entire stretch of Midtown Beach needs to close, what access will remain during construction and what the new seawall will look like.Construction is expected to begin in January 2027 and continue through summer 2028.WATCH REPORT BELOW: For people who consider Midtown Beach part of their everyday lives, a year and a half without normal access is a major concern."I hope it doesn't get higher though, I don't want to block the view," said Bridget St. Laurent, a local and owner of Palm Beach Beauty Lab on Palm Beach. "It's my life, it's my backyard, I grew up here, and the fact I can just take a five-minute drive to the ocean means so much."Those questions and concerns brought people to a public outreach meeting with project leaders."The beach, they're going to take the beach away from us. I've been there for 35 years, and there's always been a beach, and now we can't go to the beach and they can't seem to explain why they have to close the whole Midtown Beach, why can't they do it in sections," said Sheila Hurley, who lives in a condo along the beach."That's a lot of beach to close," Hurley said.Two weeks ago, the Town Council voted to replace the seawall all at once instead of completing the work in sections. The town says doing the project in sections would have taken twice as long and cost twice as much.When WPTV reporter Joel Lopez asked Hurley whether she would have been OK with that alternative, she said, "I think so, I think people would've been happier. I don't think people want the beach gone for a year and a half."Town officials say waiting to replace the seawall carries its own risks."The reason why we're doing this now is the wall is failing. If we lose the seawall in front of this condominium stretch, $7 billion of real estate is at stake. I don't see why you don't do it now," a town official said.Jake Hurley, senior project engineer and project manager for the Midtown Seawall project, told WPTV that engineering reports have found the existing seawall is at the end of its useful life."So there's a lot of different factors in that, the main being that we've had these engineering reports that support the wall's at the end of its useful life, and that's a polite way of saying that we need to replace it," Hurley said. "There's also other factors because we have just completed our renourishment cycle; we have the sand available that protects the seawall while it's being constructed."Hurley said planning has been underway for years."We've also been working on this since 2020, so we've been working on funding and a lot of the permitting efforts. So it's all led to us coming to this progressive design-build, and that's why the time is right," Hurley said.One of the biggest questions WPTV has received is whether people will still be able to use the beach during construction.Hurley said normal access to Midtown Beach will be closed because of safety concerns involving the construction site and heavy equipment."No, I don't think you're gonna want to lay on the beach while it's going on. There's gonna be some heavy equipment, but we have to close the beach access because we don't believe there's a safe way for us to bring people from the roadway onto the beach," Hurley said.However, that doesn't necessarily mean the entire shoreline will be inaccessible at all times."We can't close the ocean, so there will be times when you'll be able to traverse the beach north-south as long as you are more towards the water side," Hurley said.The space he's referring to is east of a berm that's between the ocean and construction activity. Hurley said the barrier will help protect sea turtles from entering the construction area while also keeping people away from the job site."So if you're thinking from the ocean side, it protects the wildlife, mainly the turtles, from coming into the construction site. And then the same with human wildlife, so that people aren't walking onto the construction site," Hurley said. "But no matter what construction method we end up with, there will be some kind of fencing on that side that separates the job site from the ocean."Sea turtle nesting season is also playing a major role in how the work is scheduled."Sea turtle nesting season is a major contributing factor in how we schedule the construction," Hurley said. "We cannot be on the beach unless we have a berm already constructed there."While the project is still in its design phase, Hurley said the new wall is expected to be about six inches higher on average and extend farther east than the existing wall.He also explained that the portion of the existing seawall people see today is largely decorative."The structural component of the wall is actually underground. Everything that we see above ground is decorative," Hurley said.The replacement is intended to provide more protection while maintaining the familiar look of the existing wall."So the intent is for it to be identical to what is out there. So it'll be the same color. We even went out and found the original molds that are the scallops that were put in, I think in the 80s. So it's going to look very similar to what's out there," Hurley said.Hurley said the existing above-ground wall "doesn't actually serve a purpose" and described it as sacrificial."So this new wall is going to actually provide resiliency and protect the community," Hurley said.Plans are also being considered to create walking space around the east side of the Worth Avenue clock tower.Hurley said the location of the existing seawall creates complications around the landmark."So the main reason is that the original seawall butts up directly adjacent to that, so there's no way for us to put the seawall without damaging the clock tower," Hurley said. "So we have to go seaward, and that's what we're permitted for."The project team is also recommending another beach access point on the north end of the project."We do agree that there is a lot of people who are jumping the wall. That's why we did add the, or we're recommending to add the beach access on the north end," Hurley said.The town also plans to relocate fragments of vegetation along the seawall during construction and reinstall cuttings after the replacement is complete.Phase one of the project's design is expected to be completed in fall 2026.The project's guaranteed maximum price has not yet been finalized. Hurley said the town hopes to present that figure to the Town Council in December.Construction is scheduled to begin in January 2027, with completion planned for summer 2028.Project officials plan to host more community meetings as details on the project get finalized.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

King tide flooding has been impacting roads along Flagler Drive in West Palm Beach this week, but residents on one nearby street say their problem doesn't end when the tide goes out. Neighbors on Bloomfield Drive told WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman that water can linger for hours and that they have been trying to get the city's attention over drainage concerns for years.WATCH THE FULL REPORT BELOW: Hoffman met the residents while reporting on the flooding associated with high winds and King tides.Even at low tide, he found portions of Bloomfield Drive still covered by water.For days, residents around Flagler Drive have been dealing with higher-than-normal flooding."A little hard to walk on Flagler when there's two and a half feet of water in the morning," Hampton Bebee told Hoffman.Hours after high tide, Hoffman saw water recede from many of the streets in the area.But not everywhere.On Bloomfield Drive, just off South Flagler Drive, portions of the street remained flooded.That's where Hoffman met longtime resident Alfredo Sanchez."I've lived here since '74," Sanchez told Hoffman. "I'm not going anywhere."Sanchez walked Hoffman down the street and described a problem he said residents have been dealing with for about five years.According to Sanchez, every time significant rain or king tides bring water into the area, surrounding streets can dry out while water remains on Bloomfield Drive. He said the lingering water leaves behind muck, debris and rust on sidewalks."This water shouldn't be here," Sanchez said, pointing out that it was still there six hours after high tide.For Sanchez, the water remaining at low tide is evidence of a broader drainage problem on his block."Very frustrating for that water to have been gone because it shouldn't have been there in the first place," Sanchez said. "But for that water to be there at low tide now, when it had six hours to drain out, this is the only city, the only block that does that."Sanchez told Hoffman that residents have tried to raise the issue with the city for years but have not seen a lasting resolution.Now, he is asking WPTV for help getting answers."Put some pressure on the city," Sanchez told Hoffman. "I've called the city, and we don't get any response."Hoffman reached out to the city of West Palm Beach seeking answers about the drainage problems described by residents and what can be done to address them.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Two years after her only daughter died just hours after leaving a Florida hospital, Beth Miller says she is still searching for answers.She also wants to make sure another family does not face the same barriers she has encountered.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida mom fights 'free kill' law after daughter's death"I would like to be the only one," Miller said. "I know what it feels like. I don't want anybody else to have to go through this."Miller's daughter, Dawn Miller, was 49 when she died after undergoing gallbladder surgery.A previous WPTV investigation found medical records showed Dawn initially "tolerated the procedure well." But her condition later changed.Her hemoglobin dropped. Doctors confirmed sepsis, a potentially life-threatening response to infection, and lab results the morning of her discharge showed decreased kidney function.Records also show Dawn twice resisted leaving the hospital, telling medical staff she felt "weak" and "not ready to go home."She was discharged anyway.Minutes after arriving home, she collapsed."I couldn't get her to breathe," Beth Miller recalled. "And I just felt so helpless. You know, and then you're staring at your daughter trying to do CPR, and nothing's happening."Dawn was pronounced dead about two hours after leaving the hospital.Dr. Gerald Feigin, a medical examiner and forensic pathologist who reviewed Dawn's medical records for WPTV, said he believes she should not have been discharged."She should have been given emergency transfusions and [they should] figure out why she was bleeding," Feigin said. "Possibly had additional surgery."Feigin also said the hospital should have performed an autopsy.It did not.WPTV previously reported Beth Miller requested an autopsy after her daughter's death, but the hospital declined to perform one. The hospital also declined to answer WPTV's questions about Dawn's case."I don't have an answer to this day," Miller said. "It's on your mind 24/7."Miller hoped she might find answers through the legal system.But Florida law creates another obstacle.A provision of the Florida Wrongful Death Act restricts which surviving family members can recover certain damages in medical malpractice cases.Critics have dubbed it Florida's "free kill" law.Under the provision, parents generally cannot recover certain damages for the medical malpractice death of an adult child age 25 or older. Adult children also face restrictions on recovering those damages for the death of a parent.Dawn was unmarried, in her 40s, and had no children."Unless she had kids or a spouse, there's nothing I can do," Miller said.Jordan Dulce, a West Palm Beach trial attorney who previously defended hospitals in medical malpractice cases, is among the critics calling for the law to change."It's completely arbitrary," Dulce said.Dulce said potential liability is something hospitals consider as part of risk management."I can tell you, from a risk management perspective, it's very much on their radar," he said.Critics argue the law can reduce the potential financial consequences when alleged medical negligence results in the death of certain patients compared with others.Dulce argues that it can weaken one of the financial incentives intended to promote accountability and patient safety."It's not meaning that you're intending to hurt someone," he said. "But obviously, when you don't have those guardrails up, certainly the quality of health care suffers."Florida enacted the provision in 1990 amid concerns over the cost and availability of medical malpractice insurance.Federal data show Florida had the sixth-highest number of medical malpractice claim payouts in the country that year.A Yale Journal on Regulation study also found average malpractice premiums had more than quadrupled over a four-year period, from about $4,300 to $18,000.At the time, proponents of the law argued rising malpractice costs were threatening access to doctors and driving physicians out of the state.But some of those claims later came under scrutiny.A 2003 U.S. Government Accountability Office report examined reports of physician shortages in Florida and other states and found some widely cited claims were "anecdotal" or "inaccurate."In one example, medical society officials reported two Florida counties had lost all of their neurosurgeons. GAO investigators found at least five neurosurgeons were still practicing in each county.The report also found the number of new medical licenses in Florida had increased while the number of physicians per capita remained relatively unchanged."There's been no actual studies or evidence or support for this law actually doing what it was intended to do," Dulce said.Florida's medical malpractice insurance market has since stabilized.A 2026 report from Florida's Office of Insurance Regulation found the industry was "doing well," with annual premium increases far below the triple-digit increases seen during the insurance crisis of the late 1980s.The report, however, attributed much of that stabilization to malpractice reforms enacted in 2003 — more than a decade after the wrongful-death provision took effect.Florida also remains among the most expensive states in the country for medical malpractice insurance, ranking third nationwide."No matter what we try to do to limit the victim's right to courts, that has never stopped the insurance industry from continuing to increase their prices because that's their model," Dulce said. "At the end of the day, trying to value life from the Legislature's standpoint, I think, is always improper."WPTV reached out to several local state lawmakers to share Miller's story and ask about the law. None have yet agreed to sit down for an interview.For Miller, the debate is more than a question of insurance rates, liability or state policy.It is about the daughter she still pictures lying on the floor of her home."It will always be difficult," Miller said. "I see her laying on that floor all the time."She said she will continue speaking publicly in hopes of convincing lawmakers to change the law."To get this point across, to make it so other people don't have to go through this suffering," Miller said.Last year, Florida lawmakers passed legislation that would have repealed the provision, but the bill never took effect.In the next part of WPTV's investigation, investigative reporter Kate Hussey examines what happened to that effort — and shares the stories of other Florida families who say they have encountered the same legal barrier.

A West Palm Beach woman says she knew she would have to find a health plan offered by the Affordable Care Act since her current insurance was leaving the program at the end of the year.What she didn't realize was that she was automatically signed up in a new plan.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Florida ACA customers auto-enrolled in new 2027 plans without knowing"All of a sudden I started getting phone calls, text messages, and emails from another health insurance company saying congrats, you're enrolled, and then getting a bill from them," Melissa Smith said."It took forever to figure out if my doctor was even in their network," she added. "My doctor's not in their network, so I don't want to be on their plan."What happened to Smith does appear to be common."If you were enrolled in a plan, there are automatic re-enrollments," said Scott Darius of Florida Voices for Health. "If your plan has changed or disappeared, the marketplace will often put you in a plan that they deem to be similar."It's likely enrolling in another plan on your own can clear out any automatic enrollment.Open enrollment in the ACA in Florida begins on Nov. 1.Darius says most plans have already posted their rates for 2027 and overall rates are up about 10%.He says start by finding someone you trust to help you navigate the enrollment process, which can be done at healthcare.gov "First, make a list for yourself in terms of what your priorities are," Darius said. "If you have doctors that you enjoy seeing, if you have medications that you know you need covered, create that list of priorities for yourself and then work with a trusted source to go through the options and to see what you can get covered."The enrollment period ends on Jan.

Five months after an insurance denial threatened to leave a Florida brain tumor patient facing the cost of life-saving surgery, Broqsten Bunt says he has received two pieces of news: He is medically cleared, and the nearly $1 million in medical care billed following his surgery has been wiped down to zero.WATCH FULL STORY BELOW:"Blessed to be in this position, thank you for all of your help," Bunt told investigative reporter Katie LaGrone recently. "Everything is working like it used to pre-surgery, and I've got my strength back. no future medical needs."Five months earlierWhen we first met the 36-year-old West Palm Beach man in June, his health and finances were both uncertain.Bunt is a childhood leukemia survivor. But the radiation therapy that helped rid his body of cancer as a child has taken a toll on him as an adult. He's developed an aggressive brain tumor known as a meningioma. Doctors believe it was connected to the radiation treatment he received as a child. Bunt lives in West Palm Beach. His neurosurgeon near his home said he needed to get the tumor removed and referred him to Tampa General Hospital and a specific neurosurgeon because of the complexity of his case. Then came the denialsAlthough the hospital was in-network with his insurer, Florida Blue, the surgeon was not. As a result, just before his scheduled operation, Florida Blue denied an appeal for additional coverage for the out-of-network care. In June, Bunt moved forward with the surgery anyway. He invited us to speak with him from his hospital recovery room. At the time, Bunt described being caught between his doctors and his insurance company."I'm taking calls from the insurance side, I'm taking calls from the medical office side," he told us. "I'm like, I don't write the bills, I don't pay the bills. Call each other and figure it out."Then, in the middle of the interview, Bunt's case took a dramatic turn.A Tampa General Hospital spokesperson interrupted our interview with an update, stating that hospital leadership had worked with Florida Blue and the insurer had agreed to cover Bunt's preoperative workup, surgeries, hospital admission and postoperative care. Neither Tampa General Hospital nor Florida Blue explained to us at the time what specifically prompted the reversal. Read our original investigation: Florida brain tumor patient denied insurance coverage for surgery gets full reversalFive months laterToday, Bunt said his recovery is going well, and he has been medically cleared.And when asked whether Florida Blue ultimately paid his medical bills, Bunt said, "It appears that way.""So you have zero balance?" LaGrone asked."Zero balance," Bunt said. "$993,000, almost a million dollars, is what the retail value of what was billed."Bunt said Tampa General Hospital continued working with him until his deductible was also reduced to zero. A spokesperson from TGH confirmed his insurer paid the full hospital portion of his claimFor Bunt, the resolution is remarkable. But he also believes his case illustrates how difficult it can be for a patient to challenge an insurance denial.Before the reversal, Bunt had been fighting his insurer for months over the denial. He and his wife turned to social media, appeals and eventually the news media to draw attention to his case.Bunt said he went through two denied appeals before the insurer reversed course."What really changed is when the news stepped in and created the awareness of the severity of my case," he said. "I had two appeals denied, and the condition was always the same. It didn't take any added information for them to change the denial process. It took the news making the population aware," he said.Neither Florida Blue nor Tampa General Hospital ever explained specifically why the coverage decision changed. Florida Blue told us at the time that it could not discuss individual cases but said it works with members, doctors and hospitals through its appeals process and is "pleased when we reach positive outcomes for our members." Now, with his surgery behind him and his surgery balance at zero, Bunt has a message for other patients challenging a health insurance denial."Don't back off the gas," he said. "You just have to keep pushing and keep reaching out to people. You have to get the care you need so that you can survive," he added. "You can deal with the details after. If you're not here, you don't have to worry about the details."If you are dealing with a health insurance denial over medically necessary care, let Katie know about it below.

A newly redrawn congressional district stretching across South Florida is setting up a battle between two candidates with sharply different ideas about how to make life more affordable for Floridians.Republican Casey Askar and Democrat Pia Dandiya are competing to represent District 22, which now connects coastal and inland communities across four counties.WATCH FULL REPORT BELOW: Askar, Dandiya clash over affordabilityWPTV reached out to both candidates about some of the biggest issues facing Florida voters, including affordability, insurance and health care.Dandiya agreed to an interview. For pretty much everything," Askar says in one campaign ad.The Republican has pledged to cut fuel and property taxes, increase the child tax credit and reduce government regulations he argues are contributing to higher costs.Dandiya is also making affordability a central theme of her campaign."People are no longer suffering in silence; they are suffering out loud," Dandiya told investigative reporter Kate Hussey.The candidates diverge significantly on how they would address healthcare costs.Dandiya, a former teacher and principal, supports allowing Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices and restoring Affordable Care Act subsidies as ways to lower costs."Those are real, actionable ways that we can help people make ends meet," Dandiya said.Askar is taking a different approach.On his campaign website, Askar pledges to "end Obamacare once and for all" and replace it. He also says he would target government waste and fraud while working to protect Medicare and Medicaid.Both candidates say they want to protect Social Security, but their approaches differ.Dandiya told WPTV she believes raising the cap on income subject to Social Security taxes could be one strategy for ensuring the program has enough money to pay promised benefits."People have been spending years saving into that Social Security, expecting to have a retirement in dignity," Dandiya said. "I'm a teacher and principal by trade, and I have spent my entire career serving kids and families because I know that we can do so much more for all of us."Askar has similarly positioned himself as an alternative to Washington's political establishment."We need full transparency in Congress. Casey will help deliver that," his website reads. As voters in the newly redrawn District 22 prepare to choose their next representative, the candidates are offering distinctly different solutions — but making a similar pitch: Florida families are paying too much, and Washington needs to do something about it.

Barbecue is one of the five basic food groups in Texas, and many in the Rio Grande Valley will tell you Teddy’s is one of the best BBQ joints in the state. But these days, quality meat comes with a high price, and it may impact how people vote in the midterms.“You’re talking about the cost of meat itself almost tripling, so it’s definitely been hard,” said co-owner Joel Garcia. Garcia added that every aspect of his business costs more, causing him to close on days he would like to be open and raise prices for customers.RELATED STORY | Increased beef imports still haven't brought relief for high consumer pricesAccording to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, beef prices were 3.5% higher in September 2026 than they were a year ago. Overall, the USDA expects beef prices to increase almost 9% in 2026.“It is a very fine line that we’re riding,” said Garcia. “We raise them too much, we lose customers. We keep our price too low, we lose money.”Customers are riding that same line.“A few years ago, going out was like, you know, $30,” Teddy’s BBQ customer Adolfo Grimaldo told Scripps News. “Now, it’s like $50 to $60, almost twice the price.”Menu prices are up 3.5% from last year, according to the National Restaurant Association.INTERACTIVE | A 109-year-old company is making major changes as beef prices soarWith the midterms days away, Adolfo Grimaldo thinks mixing things up, also known as ticket splitting, could be the way to bring political change and lower prices.“The way people are right now it seems everyone wants to vote one way or another, and nobody really wants to meet in the middle,” said Grimaldo. “I always like to vote for a mixture of both.”Garcia doesn’t put a lot of stock in politicians. With the American cattle herd at historic lows, his faith is in the pastures of South Texas.“I trust ranchers,” said Garcia. “I trust they are, hopefully, still continuing to produce.”Ranchers are also dealing with higher costs. Ranchers in the Rio Grande Valley told Scripps News the high price of fuel, labor, and land are all impacting their ability to grow their herd.

A Martin County judge has ordered a sentence equal to life in prison for a man who used artificial intelligence to create child pornography, a case the Martin County Sheriff's Office said it had never seen at that time.Daniel Warren was charged with 75 felony counts of possession of child pornography and seven felony counts of video voyeurism for using AI to create child pornography.WATCH REPORT BELOW:"His innocent neighbors, whose parents trusted him to be appropriate with their children, he was taking covert photos of them and then asking for those children to be transformed into some sexualized image which he shared with others," prosecutor Kristen Chase said.Warren was arrested for these crimes in 2024. At the time, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said it was their first case involving AI and child exploitation.A man who identified himself as an extended family member testified before the judge Wednesday."That would be a detriment to the children to have this man even anywhere near a child," the extended family member said.Before sentencing, Warren showed some remorse."My entire community, [I] basically destroyed every friendship I've built," Warren said. "I dwell on it every night."When his defense attorney asked whether he dwells on the decisions he made, Warren said, "Absolutely."After listening to the testimony, Judge Elizabeth Metzger decided it was not appropriate to grant a lesser sentence and opted for the minimum allowable sentence by law, at just over 1,000 months per count.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Dolly Parton's Imagination Library in Palm Beach County is seeing a boost in both donations and enrollment following WPTV's previous report on the program.After WPTV reporter Christy Waite original story aired, about 250 more children have signed up to receive free books each month, and the program has received more than $25,000 in donations.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Imagination Library sees surge after WPTV report"Since the story aired, about 250 children have signed up to receive their monthly books, and we have received more than $25,000 in donations," said Christen Thompson, director of the Palm Beach County Imagination Library.The program sends children a free, age-appropriate book each month, helping families make reading a regular part of their routine at home."There are currently 1,600 children in Palm Beach County actively enrolled and getting a free book every single month," Thompson said.Program leaders and community members hope that number keeps growing. Thompson said about 75,000 children in Palm Beach County are eligible for the program.For some families, having books at home can come with a cost that adds up."Unfortunately, for some people, books are a luxury, and this program helps take away that burden," said Merrell Angstreich, grant writer and public information officer for Lake Park.But the program's impact can go beyond the cost of a book.For mom Coral Rhodes, receiving a new book each month is an opportunity to pass the love of reading she grew up with on to her daughter."I was homeschooled growing up, and my mom loved to read, so she instilled that in me," Rhodes said. "I want to homeschool her and pass on that love of reading to her."Program leaders say more than 40,000 books have been distributed to children in Palm Beach County to date.Now, with about 250 more children signed up and more than $25,000 in new donations, leaders hope to continue growing the program and getting books into the hands of more children across Palm Beach County.Community members can also help the program work toward its goal of providing free books to every child under 5 in Palm Beach County. There are three ways to get involved: participate in the Run for Reading 5K, attend a free community movie screening, or sponsor a child for $30, which provides that child with monthly books for an entire year.

Funeral arrangements have been announced for St. Lucie County Fire District Firefighter/Paramedic Austin Hodge, who died in the line of duty on Saturday.Hodge served the St. Lucie County community for more than nine years, according to the fire district.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Services announced for St. Lucie County firefighter"The St. Lucie County Fire District continues to mourn the loss of Firefighter/Paramedic Austin Hodge," the agency said in a statement. "His loss is deeply felt by his family, friends, fellow firefighters, and the many lives he touched throughout his years of service."A public viewing will be held Friday, Nov. at River of Life Fellowship Church, located at 3950 Juanita Avenue in Fort Pierce.A memorial service will follow Saturday, Nov. at Christ Fellowship Church, located at 10250 SW Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie.The fire district said the arrangements were made in coordination with Hodge's family and Stone Brothers Funeral Home.Officials thanked the community for the support shown to Hodge's family and members of the fire district following his death."We remain grateful for the outpouring of love and support extended to Austin's family and our Fire District family during this difficult time," the agency said.The release did not provide additional details about the circumstances surrounding Hodge's death.

For the second year in a row, Spanish River High School's football team won the 6A District 14 title. The Sharks are undefeated this season against district opponents and are 5-3 overall. Two of those Sharks are now preparing to swim into deeper waters: college football.You know them from Football Night in South Florida. Derek Goulbourne and Jayden Elder are frequent visitors to WPTV's weekly highlight show. That's because they produce plays that are must-watch football.WATCH BELOW: Spanish River stars headed to Army, FIUGoulbourne, a wide receiver, is committed to play college ball for Army next year."I really like the brotherhood that they have there. They all care deeply for each other and the coaches. They want to see the best from their players," Goulbourne said.The wide receiver has only been playing on the gridiron for four years."My freshman year, so as soon as I got into high school, I got the all-clear from my mom to start playing football, so I came out to practice, and that's when it began," Goulbourne said.He is now headed to West Point on a full scholarship."I'm very thankful for the opportunity," Goulbourne said.Goulbourne said he is eager to elevate his game at the next level."I'm definitely excited. The atmosphere is definitely something crazy. I mean, playing on Saturdays with the fans on TV, that's always amazing. But I think most importantly for me, I'm focused on elevating my game to the next level, always learning new things. That's a big goal for me to go in there and learn from the veterans so that hopefully I can make an impact," Goulbourne said.He said the bond with his teammates is what he'll miss most about high school."I'm definitely going to miss just like the energy here. You know, it's like you grew up with your teammates in high school. I think that it's really great the bond that we have on this team. So I'm definitely going to miss that for sure," Goulbourne said.Like Goubourne, teammate and wide receiver Jayden Elder is also college ball bound. But Elder's football journey began when he was young."I've been playing since I was 6 years old, so that was my first ever sport I played. Ever since I started playing, I never stopped, Elder said.Once this season wraps up, Elder too will miss playing as a Spanish River Shark."The brotherhood, learning, learning from my coaches, learning from my teammates, growing, growing a bond, a connection. That's really the main thing," Elder said.After years of putting in the work, Elder earned a roster spot and committed to Florida International University."It felt like a weight lifted off my chest for sure. All the hard work I put in finally felt like it was all coming together, so it felt good for sure," Elder said.He said he hopes to carry lessons from his coach into the next level."Keeping my composure for sure, keeping my head up, don't let my chin down. Stuff like that, just staying in the game, don't let nobody bring me down," Elder said.As for this season, Goubourne has his sights set high."Definitely hope that we make a good run in the playoffs. I don't want to end the season any earlier than the state championship. So that's definitely a big goal. And I know that my teammates definitely have the same goals," Goubourne said.Head coach Nick LaSala said Goulbourne is a versatile player, and even though he is a wide receiver, he can also be used in some cases like a tight end."He knows what everybody's doing on the field. He honestly might be the smartest player on our offense. He understands the run game. He obviously understands the pass game, explosive player, physical, just a well-rounded player," LaSala said.LaSala said Goulbourne's statistics on paper don't give the entire snapshot of his type of play between downs."I think last year, his numbers, they were good, but they probably weren't reflective of how important he was to our offense and all the stuff that he did," LaSala said.It's not a secret college recruitment can be a long and big process to take on, especially for high school student-athletes. But LaSala is there to do what he can, advocating for his players."I mean, you have the conversations with the college coaches in the offseason about all these different guys," LaSala said.Using film has been a big component of showcasing Goulbourne and Elder's skills on the field, LaSala said."Sometimes you just have to laugh at it because I get to see it on the practice field every day. But when they (college coaches) can't see it, all they can trust is the film. So there's definitely been a lot of that, and they've both done a good job of putting it on film," LaSala said.LaSala also shared the advice he has for Goulbourne and Elder as they take their football careers to the college level next year."If you just focus on being there and growing in the program and being invested in the people around you, it's going to work out for yourself because the rooms now in college, they change so quickly, which honestly, being in South Florida, they probably get a taste of that as well because South Florida invented the transfer portal," LaSala said.LaSala advises the players to simply take it all in, for all its worth, and to "just be where your feet are."The Spanish River Sharks round out the regular season with a game this Friday and will have their final home game on Nov.

Local food makers, artists and community organizations are getting a new waterfront showcase in Jupiter as Charlie & Joe's at Love Street launches a series of events designed to support local vendors and bring families together.The first Heart & Harvest market is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. at Love Street in Jupiter.Lucky Shuck Executive Chef John Daly told WPTV the event is focused on supporting the people who live and work in the community."It's all about supporting local, our local vendors, our local fishermen," Daly said during WPTV’s Shining A Light. "[It's a] good way to bring out the family, enjoy the outdoors, and come get a bite to eat."Schedule of Events• Saturday, Nov. to 2 p.m.: Taste of the Inlet – Heart & Harvest (green market)• Sunday, Nov. to 2 p.m.: Art in the Heart – Holiday Edition• Sunday, Dec. to 2 p.m.: Taste of the Inlet – Christmas Market at Love StreetAmong the vendors participating is Danielle Sarette of Seaside Sourdough.Sarette makes sourdough products from her home in Jupiter Farms and told WPTV that her children have become part of the family baking experience."My children love to come out with us to the vendors [to] the markets and be able to experience the joy that I have with [baking], and as well as baking with me," Sarette said. "(My kids) help me with the bread, the bagels, focaccia, everything that we make from scratch."Sarette also told WPTV that Seaside Sourdough recently launched a website, Seaside Sourdough.The market-style setting also provides a platform for The Arc of Palm Beach County's artisan program.Sean Stickley, the organization’s artisan program manager, showed WPTV artwork designed and assembled with adults participating in the program."Everything here is designed and put together with our adults, and they will get a commission check," Stickley said.The artwork provides another way for shoppers to support people in the community while looking for gifts ahead of the holidays.Stickley invited visitors to see the work in person, adding, "Hopefully you'll come out and see us and buy some stuff for Christmas or the holidays."Heart & Harvest is part of the larger "Events in the Heart" series at Charlie & Joe's at Love Street.According to event organizers, the series is built around four themes: Taste of the Inlet, Art in the Heart, Wellness in the Heart and Music in the Heart.The programming is intended to bring food, art, fitness and entertainment to the waterfront while giving local vendors and community groups opportunities to connect with visitors.That local connection is particularly timely heading into the holidays, when markets such as Heart & Harvest can introduce shoppers to small businesses and local artists while giving families another reason to spend time together outdoors.Heart & Harvest is scheduled for Saturday, Nov. at Charlie & Joe's at Love Street, 1116 Love St. in Jupiter.The broader Events in the Heart series is free and open to the community, although organizers say some individual activities and experiences may require advance registration and an additional fee.More information about upcoming events is available on the Love Street events page.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Email me at tawalker@wptv.com.

King tides are pushing water onto roads across the Treasure Coast , and forecasters say the high water isn’t done yet. The National Weather Service extended a coastal flood warning for Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties until 2 a.m. The warning first took effect early Sunday and was originally set to expire Monday night. In Sewall’s Point, Sewall’s Point Road was completely flooded Wednesday. Cars and trucks crawled through the water, and several vehicles got stuck. Gina Rossi-Scheiman lives just around the corner. She has dealt with king tides before, but she says nothing like this. The flooding is really bad right now. I didn’t expect it to be this bad where I’m really not comfortable going down the road, Rossi-Scheiman said. She said Sewall’s Point Road is narrow to begin with, which makes the flooding harder to get around. The road isn’t this bad often, but when it is, you really can’t be out in it, she said. If your car is lower to the ground, you can’t drive in it at all. She worries her car could stall in the water and that the saltwater will damage it, so she plans to stay home unless she has to go out. The flooding stretched well beyond Sewall’s Point . Parts of South Hutchinson Island were underwater, and Northeast Indian River Drive flooded during high tide. In Palm City, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding along Southwest Dyer Point Road, Southwest 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. In Fort Pierce, the high water carried a dumpster out into the water. King tides are exceptionally high tides that happen around a full or new moon, when the pull of the sun and moon line up and lift the water higher than usual. This round came around Sunday night’s full moon. Strong onshore winds piled even more water against the coast, sending it over seawalls and into low-lying neighborhoods. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana Some relief is on the way, but not right away. CBS12 meteorologists expect the winds to ease through the rest of the week. Even with calmer conditions, the tides will stay high enough to keep pushing water into flood-prone streets around high tide. The weather service warns that coastal roads may close and that low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure could flood. Forecasters also expect significant shoreline erosion. Coastal flooding is occurring or imminent, the weather service said in its latest statement. The beaches remain dangerous as well. A high surf advisory is in effect until 2 a.m. Friday, with breaking waves of 7 to 11 feet. A high rip current risk runs through late Friday night, and forecasters urge swimmers to stay out of the water. Rossi-Scheiman is finding some humor in it. She joked that her husband, who drives a low car, might have to sleep at work. But that’d be okay with me, she said. Officials urge drivers to stay off flooded roads, since there’s no telling how deep the water is.

Developer Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County in support of restoring the St. Lucie River.The developer said the parcel was donated from the northern section of the Newfield development to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, a federal plan to restore, protect, and preserve South Florida's water resources.WATCH REPORT BELOW: James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the land will have the capacity to host large amounts of muck that will need to be dredged out of the St. Lucie River to improve water quality. Fitzgerald said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres. Combined, Fitzgerald said the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck from the river.WPTV asked Fitzgerald what happens to the muck after the removal project."The muck will dry out, and we're hoping at some point in the future that land can be used as a recreational project," Fitzgerald said. "Or perhaps, depending on the needs of the county, in some other future environmental restoration projects."Fitzgerald said the project to remove the muck will begin once federal funding is authorized.

Nearly eight years after WPTV first investigated concerns about a possible cluster of glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County, health officials have reviewed the numbers again.The latest findings show the number of cases remains in line with what would be expected based on the county's population, but families who lost loved ones to the deadly brain cancer say important questions remain unanswered.WATCH THE REPORT BELOW: The latest review by the Florida Department of Health follows years of WPTV reporting into concerns raised by patients and families who discovered they lived near others diagnosed with the same aggressive form of brain cancer.While health officials say the data does not show a statistically significant increase in cases, the review does not examine whether patients were concentrated on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods.For families who have spent years searching for answers, that distinction matters.READ THE FULL STATE REPORT BELOW: A young man's death helped spark an investigationFor Deb Johnston, the loss of her son, Lenny Schelin Jr., is still painful."It's been eight years since Lenny passed," she said.Lenny was just 33 years old when he died from glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer.He was healthy, active and loved fishing. He survived just 17 months after his diagnosis."Everybody loved Lenny. He just had this charm about him," his mother recalled.Lenny's story was among the first that helped WPTV uncover concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Other patients included Mark Cunningham, who was also in his 30s, and Kyle Vericella, who was just 18.After WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts uncovered the local cases, dozens of additional patients and family members contacted her with their stories.Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns.Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, making the younger ages of some patients particularly troubling to their families.But it wasn't just their ages that raised questions.As patients began connecting with one another, WPTV mapped where they lived beginning in 2018.Some lived within blocks of one another. Others lived on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home.The reporting drew attention from lawmakers, environmental advocate Erin Brockovich and the Florida Department of Health.What did the original 2019 investigation find?The concerns prompted health officials to examine glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County."You brought it to my attention. It was alarming; it was nerve-wracking," Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, told WPTV's Meghan McRoberts.Sperber said the concerns led to a request for assistance from Florida's cancer registry."I asked for assistance from our cancer registry through our leadership, my boss," he said. "And we were able to help collect a lot of information."That information was compiled into a report released in 2019.Despite concerns about the number of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, the report did not find a statistically significant increase in cases that would warrant a more intensive investigation.Health officials also reviewed existing environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area's power plant.Sperber pointed to ongoing environmental monitoring as part of the state's assessment."There is water testing, there is vegetation testing, they look at watermelon, milk, fish, soil, they would know if there is any release of radiation," Sperber said.The findings were disappointing for families who had hoped the investigation would uncover an explanation."I was like deflated because we worked so hard," Johnston said.What does the latest glioblastoma review show?Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Their conclusion remains largely unchanged."The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today," Sperber told WPTV. "We are seeing the same ratio, the same expected number of cases that we would expect statewide for our county."According to Sperber, a county with approximately 400,000 residents would be expected to see about 14 to 15 new glioblastoma diagnoses each year.The report also shows that from 2019 to 2023, there were 95 cases of glioblastoma, just three cases more than the 92 expected.Health officials say the latest review does not identify an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases compared with statewide expectations.Unlike the 2019 report, however, the latest review does not break down cases by age or sex.Officials say there are too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable.The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records without identifying new concerns.What questions remain?Although the latest review did not find an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases countywide, it does not settle every question raised by patients and their families.Sperber acknowledged the analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods.That means the review's broader findings do not necessarily address the geographic patterns that originally concerned families, determining what causes glioblastoma is also challenging.Sperber pointed to recent research by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences identifying nearly a dozen potential factors associated with the disease, making it difficult to identify a single environmental source."I wish there was an answer," Sperber said. "I wish there was a smoking gun that says okay here is the reason, the cause, the source for glioblastoma."As St. Lucie County's population continues to grow, health officials expect the total number of diagnoses to rise as well.But for families who lost loved ones, the question remains whether the countywide numbers tell the entire story.A mother's call for a closer look at her hometownFor Johnston, hearing that the state's findings have not changed was difficult."I was deflated when you told me that. Palm Beach County sheriff's deputies discharged their firearms following a hours-long negotiation with an armed person who was threatening suicide Wednesday night, according to the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office.WATCH: Sheriff Ric Bradshaw gives update on fatal shootingDeputies responded shortly before 10 p.m. Wednesday to Sandalfoot Square at 23066 State Road 7 near Boca Raton, after receiving a call from relatives of an armed man who "was very suicidal," Sheriff Ric Bradshaw said Thursday during a press conference.Deputies arrived to find Joshua Senfeld, a 30-year-old Army veteran sitting on the ground in front of the open driver's side door of his car, leaning back against the running board, with a gun in his left hand. He repeatedly put the weapon to his head during the standoff, the sheriff said."He said, 'I want to die. I want to kill myself,'" Bradshaw said. He put it to his head several times." According to PBSO, deputies spent several hours negotiating with Senfeld, who suffered from PTSD and had been drinking, from 9:55 p.m. before the incident resulted in deputies firing their weapons."They talked to this guy a long, long time, trying to talk him down. Even one of our guys who's a vet kind of connected with him a little bit and told them, 'Hey, you know, we're going to get you the help you need,'" Bradshaw said. "But it was pretty obvious he's decided that this was the end of the day for him, and then that's when he made his move and they had to do what they had to do." The sheriff said the man became agitated and began to stand up with the gun in a "ready position." Deputies, perceiving a threat, opened fire."I would characterize that the gun was in a ready position. Yes, that's what I would characterize it as. He's obviously making an assertive, aggressive mood coming off the ground with the gun in the ready position," Bradshaw said.Deputies immediately attempted CPR and called fire rescue to the scene, but the man died, the sheriff said.The gun recovered appeared to be a 9mm handgun with an extended magazine, which holds more rounds than a standard magazine, the sheriff said. When asked whether the man pointed the gun at deputies or fired at them, Bradshaw said Senfeld did not shoot back and that deputies did not wait for him to do so."No, no, they didn't give him that opportunity," he said. "See, that's the idea, when people present to you that you're going to be in jeopardy, you don't have to wait till they shoot at you. That's not smart."The sheriff said he could not yet confirm the origin of what appeared to be bullet holes in one of the agency's cruisers that was towed from the scene, saying he had not yet spoken with investigators about it.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement is investigating the shooting. The deputies involved are on paid administrative leave as the investigation continues, the sheriff said.

Women's hockey is growing in South Florida, from the pee-wee level all the way up to the college level, and the University of Miami Women's Hockey Club team is part of that surge.Head coach Justina Holland, a former player, rebooted the women's hockey club program at the University of Miami in 2021. A data breach involving a Florida student financial aid website may have exposed personal information, including Social Security numbers, belonging to approximately 4.9 million people, according to the Florida Department of Education (FLDOE).WATCH REPORT BELOW: FLDOE said in a Thursday statement that staff became aware Oct. 19 of unauthorized criminal access involving its Florida Student Financial Aid website.The department said the compromised personally identifiable information included Social Security numbers. Officials did not specify what other types of personal information may have been exposed.The breach is believed to have been limited to the Florida Student Financial Aid website, and as many as 4.9 million people potentially were affected, according to FLDOE.The department said it activated its cybersecurity response protocols after detecting the incident, took steps to contain the unauthorized activity and secure its systems, and notified the Florida Attorney General's Office.FLDOE said it is working with the Florida Digital Service and Florida Department of Law Enforcement. The incident remains under criminal investigation.FLDOE said current financial aid is not at risk and the incident will not delay financial aid disbursements or tuition payments from the department.Officials also said the breach will not affect eligibility for scholarships, grants or student loans from FLDOE.Some department websites and online services, however, may experience temporary disruptions as officials work to restore full functionality.FLDOE recommends monitoring financial and online accounts for suspicious activity and regularly reviewing account statements and credit reports.The department also recommends considering a fraud alert or credit freeze with the major credit bureaus. Consumers can obtain free credit reports through AnnualCreditReport.com and find additional information about responding to a data breach through the Federal Trade Commission's IdentityTheft.gov website.Anyone with questions about the FLDOE breach can contact the department at databreach@fldoe.org.FLDOE said information could change as the criminal investigation continues. The department is posting updates on its data breach information page.

When Jensen Beach needs a big play, senior Alex Thornton has a knack for delivering on both sides of the football. Thornton is this week’s CBS12 News Athlete of the Week after a career night helped the Falcons capture the District 13-4A football championship outright. In a 42-21 victory over Fort Pierce Westwood on October 23, Thornton rushed for 215 yards on just 15 carries and scored four touchdowns. He found the end zone on runs of 2, 39, 20 and 7 yards, recording the first four-touchdown game of his career. Three of those scores came in the second half as Jensen Beach pulled away. But Thornton’s impact extends well beyond the offensive backfield. A physical, hard-hitting linebacker, he has built a reputation for setting the tone on defense. His ability to make plays at both running back and linebacker has made him one of Jensen Beach’s most important players. He is the tone-setter, head coach Tim Caffey said in an earlier profile of Thornton, describing the senior’s physical style of play. See also: Dolphins look to build on first win against Patriots Thornton’s contributions are part of a larger winning tradition at Jensen Beach. The Falcons’ victory over Westwood secured the program’s fifth district championship overall and fourth in the past five years under Caffey. It also extended the team’s streak of playoff appearances to five consecutive seasons. Thornton has been part of three district championship teams during his high school career, making him a key figure in the program’s continued success. His potential has also attracted attention at the next level. Before his senior season, Thornton had received eight Division I college football offers, according to TCPalm’s recruiting profile. With the district title secured, Thornton and the Falcons now turn their attention to the postseason. For the senior, the goal is to help Jensen Beach make another deep playoff run before his high school career comes to an end. Thornton’s performance against Westwood showed exactly what makes him stand out: the ability to take over a game, lead by example and deliver when his team needs him most. King tides are pushing water onto roads across the Treasure Coast , and forecasters say the high water isn’t done yet. The National Weather Service extended a coastal flood warning for Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties until 2 a.m. The warning first took effect early Sunday and was originally set to expire Monday night. In Sewall’s Point, Sewall’s Point Road was completely flooded Wednesday. Cars and trucks crawled through the water, and several vehicles got stuck. Gina Rossi-Scheiman lives just around the corner. She has dealt with king tides before, but she says nothing like this. The flooding is really bad right now. I didn’t expect it to be this bad where I’m really not comfortable going down the road, Rossi-Scheiman said. She said Sewall’s Point Road is narrow to begin with, which makes the flooding harder to get around. The road isn’t this bad often, but when it is, you really can’t be out in it, she said. If your car is lower to the ground, you can’t drive in it at all. She worries her car could stall in the water and that the saltwater will damage it, so she plans to stay home unless she has to go out. The flooding stretched well beyond Sewall’s Point . Parts of South Hutchinson Island were underwater, and Northeast Indian River Drive flooded during high tide. In Palm City, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported significant flooding along Southwest Dyer Point Road, Southwest 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. In Fort Pierce, the high water carried a dumpster out into the water. King tides are exceptionally high tides that happen around a full or new moon, when the pull of the sun and moon line up and lift the water higher than usual. This round came around Sunday night’s full moon. Strong onshore winds piled even more water against the coast, sending it over seawalls and into low-lying neighborhoods. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana Some relief is on the way, but not right away. CBS12 meteorologists expect the winds to ease through the rest of the week. Even with calmer conditions, the tides will stay high enough to keep pushing water into flood-prone streets around high tide. The weather service warns that coastal roads may close and that low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure could flood. Forecasters also expect significant shoreline erosion. Coastal flooding is occurring or imminent, the weather service said in its latest statement. The beaches remain dangerous as well. A high surf advisory is in effect until 2 a.m. Friday, with breaking waves of 7 to 11 feet. A high rip current risk runs through late Friday night, and forecasters urge swimmers to stay out of the water. Rossi-Scheiman is finding some humor in it. She joked that her husband, who drives a low car, might have to sleep at work. But that’d be okay with me, she said. Officials urge drivers to stay off flooded roads, since there’s no telling how deep the water is.

James Martin, a lifelong Martin County resident and Coast Guard veteran, has announced his candidacy for Congress, citing rising costs and quality-of-life issues as key reasons for entering the race. "One, tackle the cost-of-living crisis. Two, clean up our water once and for all. And three, get big money out of politics," Martin said. Martin, whose family has lived in the area for four generations, previously worked in the White House for former Vice President Kamala Harris and is a husband and father to two young daughters. He believes federal economic policies are contributing to higher prices for families. "We need to repeal what are, in my view, reckless, blanket tariffs, which are driving up the costs of everything from groceries to household goods," he said. Martin credited his opponent, Congressman Brian Mast, with raising awareness about clean waterways but said he would fight to complete Everglades restoration and stop toxic discharges from Lake Okeechobee into the St. Lucie Estuary and Indian River Lagoon. "You shouldn't have to wonder how your member of Congress is going to vote on clean water or the environment based on who the president is, who their donors are, and what's in their stock portfolio," Martin said. "In my view, Brian Mast has taken several bad votes not only with the environment at large but also when it comes to clean water." Clean water is also a top priority for Independent candidate Alex Cooke, a former mayor of Juno Beach, local businessman, and foster parent. Cooke said he wants to end Lake Okeechobee discharges and restore natural water flows to the Everglades. "We can definitely do a better job controlling the flows to the south and working to better create flows in and out of Lake Okeechobee," Cooke said. "It's time to go back to the way nature intended it, with the Everglades being the cleaning system for our waterways." "I would bring funding back here to help with the affordability crisis, specifically with property insurance. We should expand a sinking fund but at a federal level," Cooke said. Get the latest political updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Cooke said his experience outside of politics sets him apart from the other candidates. "Of the three candidates in this race, I am the only one with a real job outside of politics," Cooke said. "We're basically talking career politicians. You want something different, you've got to look at the game differently. I don't consider it my career. I consider it an opportunity to fix the way things are going and move on." While Martin has never held elected office, he pointed to his military and White House experience as preparation for Congress.

Florida health officials released an updated Treasure Coast brain cancer review Thursday, finding no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in the areas examined. But families who have spent years tracking brain tumor diagnoses say the review still does not answer all of their questions particularly about patients living on the same streets or just doors apart. This upsets me, said Stephanie Ankiel, with the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast. I see family after family, and when is it enough? Like, when do we actually look into this problem? The findings come as the CBS12 News I-Team continues pressing the Florida Department of Health for updated data and answers about which brain tumors are counted. CBS12 News has covered families’ concerns for well over a decade. The analysis covers diagnoses through 2023, leaving more recent cases outside its scope. It also documents a change in the tumor classifications included compared with the state’s 2019 review. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber directed the I-Team to the report, accompanying resources and a scientific journal article addressing environmental risk factors. I am hopeful that, after reviewing the website and the available documents, you will find reassurance in the thorough work conducted by our public health scientists, Sperber wrote. What the state found The updated assessment examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 2014 through 2023 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties, along with three St. Officials compared recorded diagnoses with the number expected based on statewide cancer rates, accounting for age. Lucie County, the state recorded 95 diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected. Across the full decade, the ZIP code analysis found: 34952: 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected. 34983: 21 diagnoses, compared with approximately 20 expected. 34982: 12 diagnoses, compared with approximately 13 expected. None showed a statistically significant excess. Officials said small case numbers can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase the number of diagnoses without an increase in underlying risk. The report does not determine what caused individual patients’ cancers. Questions beyond glioblastoma Ankiel said she was not surprised by the state’s conclusion. Earlier this month, she drove I-Team reporter Katie Bente through Fort Pierce neighborhoods, pointing out homes where she said brain tumor patients had lived in some cases, only doors apart. Her questions are also personal. Ankiel’s husband, Mark Cunningham, was initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma in 2012. Ankiel said his cancer was later diagnosed as glioblastoma. Now, Ankiel is helping another patient with the same initial diagnosis. Amber Lee, 37, is living with oligodendroglioma, a brain tumor that is distinct from glioblastoma. The first thing I remember thinking of when they told me I had cancer was, I have a daughter, Lee said. Lee also grew up in the same Fort Pierce neighborhood as Ankiel’s husband. I realized that a lot of those people were family members of people that I grew up with, people that my family, my parents grew up with, Lee said. The shared diagnosis and neighborhood history do not establish a common cause or prove a cancer cluster. But Ankiel believes the geographic patterns deserve a closer examination. The state analyzed entire ZIP codes, not individual streets. Maybe the ZIP codes are a little bit too broad, Ankiel said. Let’s actually, let’s look at some of the streets. Why oligodendroglioma was not counted The updated review focuses specifically on glioblastoma. It excludes oligodendroglioma the tumor Lee is living with and the tumor Ankiel said her husband was initially diagnosed with. The report shows two tumor classification codes included in the state’s 2019 analysis 9450 and 9451 were excluded from the new review. The department said medical classifications have evolved and those oligodendroglioma codes are no longer included in the current glioblastoma definition. The I-Team previously asked health officials how their analysis handles patients whose diagnoses change and whether other brain cancers were examined separately. The report does not explain how a case initially classified as oligodendroglioma and later diagnosed as glioblastoma would be counted. Recent diagnoses fall outside the review The assessment does not include diagnoses from 2024 through 2026. An accompanying FAQ says 2023 was the latest finalized cancer registry year available. Officials said the reporting delay allows records to be checked for completeness and accuracy. Lee’s diagnosis falls outside the period examined. Her tumor also would not be included in the glioblastoma analysis because it is classified as oligodendroglioma. Lee said she wants officials to continue studying brain tumor diagnoses in the area. She is especially concerned about her younger sister, who grew up in the same home. I want to know if my sister can get tested somehow before it’s too late for her, Lee said. The review also does not capture more recent glioblastoma diagnoses previously covered by the I-Team. Florida health officials released an updated Treasure Coast brain cancer review Thursday, finding no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in the areas examined. But families who have spent years tracking brain tumor diagnoses say the review still does not answer all of their questions particularly about patients living on the same streets or just doors apart. This upsets me, said Stephanie Ankiel, with the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast. I see family after family, and when is it enough? Like, when do we actually look into this problem? The findings come as the CBS12 News I-Team continues pressing the Florida Department of Health for updated data and answers about which brain tumors are counted. CBS12 News has covered families’ concerns for well over a decade. The analysis covers diagnoses through 2023, leaving more recent cases outside its scope. It also documents a change in the tumor classifications included compared with the state’s 2019 review. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber directed the I-Team to the report, accompanying resources and a scientific journal article addressing environmental risk factors. I am hopeful that, after reviewing the website and the available documents, you will find reassurance in the thorough work conducted by our public health scientists, Sperber wrote. Lucie County, the state recorded 95 diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected. Across the full decade, the ZIP code analysis found: 34952: 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected. 34983: 21 diagnoses, compared with approximately 20 expected. 34982: 12 diagnoses, compared with approximately 13 expected. None showed a statistically significant excess. Officials said small case numbers can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase the number of diagnoses without an increase in underlying risk. Earlier this month, she drove I-Team reporter Katie Bente through Fort Pierce neighborhoods, pointing out homes where she said brain tumor patients had lived in some cases, only doors apart. The first thing I remember thinking of when they told me I had cancer was, I have a daughter, Lee said. Lee also grew up in the same Fort Pierce neighborhood as Ankiel’s husband. I realized that a lot of those people were family members of people that I grew up with, people that my family, my parents grew up with, Lee said. The shared diagnosis and neighborhood history do not establish a common cause or prove a cancer cluster. But Ankiel believes the geographic patterns deserve a closer examination.
