Officials said the reporting delay allows records to be checked for completeness and accuracy. Lee’s diagnosis falls outside the period examined. Her tumor also would not be included in the glioblastoma analysis because it is classified as oligodendroglioma. Lee said she wants officials to continue studying brain tumor diagnoses in the area. She is especially concerned about her younger sister, who grew up in the same home. I want to know if my sister can get tested somehow before it’s too late for her, Lee said. Nearly eight years after WFLX first investigated concerns about a possible cluster of glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County, health officials have reviewed the numbers again. The latest findings show the number of cases remains in line with what would be expected based on the county’s population, but families who lost loved ones to the deadly brain cancer say important questions remain unanswered. The latest review by the Florida Department of Health follows years of WFLX reporting into concerns raised by patients and families who discovered they lived near others diagnosed with the same aggressive form of brain cancer. While health officials say the data does not show a statistically significant increase in cases, the review does not examine whether patients were concentrated on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods. For families who have spent years searching for answers, that distinction matters. A young man’s death helped spark an investigation For Deb Johnston, the loss of her son, Lenny Schelin Jr., is still painful. “It’s been eight years since Lenny passed,” she said. Lenny was just 33 years old when he died from glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer. He was healthy, active and loved fishing. He survived just 17 months after his diagnosis. He just had this charm about him,” his mother recalled. Lenny’s story was among the first that helped WPTV uncover concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. Other patients included Mark Cunningham, who was also in his 30s, and Kyle Vericella, who was just 18. After WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts uncovered the local cases, dozens of additional patients and family members contacted her with their stories. Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns. Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, making the younger ages of some patients particularly troubling to their families. But it wasn’t just their ages that raised questions. As patients began connecting with one another, WPTV mapped where they lived beginning in 2018. Some lived within blocks of one another. Others lived on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home. The reporting drew attention from lawmakers, environmental advocate Erin Brockovich and the Florida Department of Health. What did the original 2019 investigation find? The concerns prompted health officials to examine glioblastoma cases in St. “You brought it to my attention. It was alarming; it was nerve-wracking,” Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, told WPTV’s Meghan McRoberts. Sperber said the concerns led to a request for assistance from Florida’s cancer registry. “I asked for assistance from our cancer registry through our leadership, my boss,” he said. “And we were able to help collect a lot of information.” That information was compiled into a report released in 2019. Despite concerns about the number of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, the report did not find a statistically significant increase in cases that would warrant a more intensive investigation. Health officials also reviewed existing environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area’s power plant. Sperber pointed to ongoing environmental monitoring as part of the state’s assessment. “There is water testing, there is vegetation testing, they look at watermelon, milk, fish, soil, they would know if there is any release of radiation,” Sperber said. The findings were disappointing for families who had hoped the investigation would uncover an explanation. “I was like deflated because we worked so hard,” Johnston said. What does the latest glioblastoma review show? Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Their conclusion remains largely unchanged. “The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today,” Sperber told WPTV. “We are seeing the same ratio, the same expected number of cases that we would expect statewide for our county.” According to Sperber, a county with approximately 400,000 residents would be expected to see about 14 to 15 new glioblastoma diagnoses each year. The report also shows that from 2019 to 2023, there were 95 cases of glioblastoma, just three cases more than the 92 expected. Health officials say the latest review does not identify an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases compared with statewide expectations. Unlike the 2019 report, however, the latest review does not break down cases by age or sex. Officials say there are too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable. The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records without identifying new concerns. Although the latest review did not find an unusual increase in glioblastoma cases countywide, it does not settle every question raised by patients and their families. Sperber acknowledged the analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods. That means the review’s broader findings do not necessarily address the geographic patterns that originally concerned families, determining what causes glioblastoma is also challenging. Sperber pointed to recent research by the International Journal of Molecular Sciences identifying nearly a dozen potential factors associated with the disease, making it difficult to identify a single environmental source. “I wish there was an answer,” Sperber said. “I wish there was a smoking gun that says okay here is the reason, the cause, the source for glioblastoma.” As St. Lucie County’s population continues to grow, health officials expect the total number of diagnoses to rise as well. But for families who lost loved ones, the question remains whether the countywide numbers tell the entire story. A mother’s call for a closer look at her hometown For Johnston, hearing that the state’s findings have not changed was difficult. “I was deflated when you told me that. I was like, oh my God,” she told McRoberts. She remains grateful that health officials are continuing to review the numbers. When asked whether she was glad the state was still looking into the issue, she responded, “Yes … it gives you hope for the others that come behind us.” But she wants investigators to look more closely at individual neighborhoods, rather than relying on broader geographic data. When McRoberts asked where she would like additional testing conducted, her answer was immediate. “In the White City area,” she said. Nearly eight years after losing her son, Deb says the search for answers has taken an emotional toll. “I haven’t given up; it’s just you get tired,” she said. Millions invested in glioblastoma research Since WPTV’s initial reporting, the Florida Department of Health has invested at least $9 million in glioblastoma research. Deb has also worked to support research in her son’s memory. Each year, she hosts a fishing tournament honoring Lenny, who loved spending time on the water. The event has raised nearly $300,000 for glioblastoma research. Another tournament is approaching, continuing her efforts to help other families facing the same devastating diagnosis. For Deb, the hope is that continued research and closer examination of local cases will eventually provide answers. “I’m just glad you have followed through the way that you have,” she told McRoberts. King tides and strong onshore winds have caused significant coastal erosion along the boardwalk in Vero Beach, with officials describing the damage as severe and warning that the weather event is not yet over. I was trying to look it up to see if there was a name, a named storm off the coast or anything, but nope, it's just weather," one observer said. Quintin Bergman is the resource manager with Indian River County. He's monitoring the situation. "So, what we're seeing here is two weather events that have aligned," Bergman said. "We're still in the middle of this. We're not through with the weather event. The forecast is showing elevated winds for a few more days, and the king tide event is still going to be affecting the tide." The erosion has impacted a section of beachfront parking on Ocean Drive, an area official have identified as one of their erosion hot spots. One couple who walked on the beach the day before said they didn’t notice the damage but weren’t surprised by the situation. "That's what nature wants to do, and that's kind of what you need to let nature do, I think. But the problem is we keep building on it. That's the interruption, not nature doing its thing," they said. Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Officials described the erosion as approaching severe. "I would classify this as leaning more on the severe side of erosion. It's not extreme by any means, but definitely we are very concerned," Bergman said. Authorities are contacting park officials to discuss safety measures to protect the public. Lucie County, beach erosion has also been observed, but officials credited beach replenishment projects with helping protect nearby buildings. "I mean, it certainly helped that we did a renourishment last year. Any time you lose sand, the more you have on there, the better you're going to protect your shoreline," Erick Gill, St. Lucie County public information officer, said. In parts of Martin County, residents are still dealing with flooding caused by the rough conditions. Despite the challenges, some beachgoers in Vero Beach, like Svetlana Ryan, are still enjoying the view and noting the changes to the shoreline. "We noticed because there was so much sand before, and now it's just a wall. But you do with whatever you have to do here in Vero Beach," Ryan said. Officials plan to assess the damage after the weather event passes. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

hero.headline: Indian River County early voting ends Saturday ahead of Tuesday election
hero.body:
Early voting ends Saturday in Indian River County, ahead of Election Day on Tuesday, Nov. 3. Voters casting ballots during early voting may use any open early voting site in their county.

On Election Day, polls will open at 7 a.m., and voters must cast their ballots at their assigned polling place. Voters can check their polling location, sample ballot and county-specific voting information through their Supervisor of Elections office before heading out.

Vote-by-mail ballots must reach the local elections office by 7 p.m. on Election Day to be counted.

The ballot includes statewide contests for governor, U.S. Senate and attorney general. Republican Byron Donalds faces Democrat David Jolly for governor, Republican Ashley Moody faces Democrat Angie Nixon for U.S. Senate, and Republican James Uthmeier faces Democrat Jose Javier Rodriguez for attorney general. Congressional and state legislative races also will appear on ballots. Local races and ballot questions depend on a voter’s address.

Voters also will decide Amendment 3, which would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes and lower the annual cap on assessment increases for certain non-homestead properties. The proposal also would limit how local governments can use property tax revenue. Supporters say it would provide tax relief, while local governments and public agencies have warned it could reduce funding for services. A proposed constitutional amendment needs at least 60% voter approval to pass.

hero.headline: Updated state review finds St. Lucie County glioblastoma cases in line with expectations
hero.body:
An updated Florida Department of Health review released Thursday found no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in St. Lucie County, where families have spent years raising concerns about brain tumor diagnoses. The state recorded 95 diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected based on age-adjusted statewide cancer rates. The review covers diagnoses through 2023 and focuses specifically on glioblastoma, excluding oligodendroglioma. Its geographic analysis examines entire ZIP codes, while Fort Pierce families continue asking officials to examine patients who lived on the same streets.

The assessment examined glioblastoma diagnoses from 2014 through 2023 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties. Across that decade, ZIP code 34952 had 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected; 34983 had 21, compared with approximately 20 expected; and 34982 had 12, compared with approximately 13 expected. Officials found each ZIP code’s count statistically in line with expectations. They said small case counts can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase diagnoses without increasing the underlying risk.

Stephanie Ankiel, with the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast, wants a closer examination of geographic patterns. She has pointed to homes in Fort Pierce neighborhoods where she said brain tumor patients lived, sometimes only doors apart. Her husband, Mark Cunningham, was initially diagnosed with oligodendroglioma in 2012, and Ankiel said his cancer was later diagnosed as glioblastoma. Ankiel is now helping Amber Lee, 37, who has oligodendroglioma and grew up in the same Fort Pierce neighborhood as Cunningham. Those connections alone do not establish a common cause or prove a cancer cluster.

The updated review excludes tumor classification codes 9450 and 9451, which were included in the state’s 2019 analysis. The department said medical classifications have evolved and those oligodendroglioma codes fall outside the current glioblastoma definition. Lee’s diagnosis also falls after the review period. An accompanying FAQ identifies 2023 as the latest finalized cancer registry year and says the reporting delay allows records to be checked for completeness and accuracy.

The Florida Cancer Data System generally records patients’ addresses at diagnosis, which may differ from where they lived years earlier or experienced a potentially relevant exposure. Health officials also reviewed public drinking-water records, available private-well data and radiation monitoring around the St. Lucie nuclear power plant. The department said it will continue monitoring cancer incidence and working with state and local partners. Ankiel said she wants to work with health officials as families continue seeking answers about neighborhood patterns.
hero.article_text: Florida health officials released an updated Treasure Coast brain cancer review Thursday, finding no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in the areas examined. But families who have spent years tracking brain tumor diagnoses say the review still does not answer all of their questions particularly about patients living on the same streets or just doors apart. This upsets me, said Stephanie Ankiel, with the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast. I see family after family, and when is it enough? Like, when do we actually look into this problem? The findings come as the CBS12 News I-Team continues pressing the Florida Department of Health for updated data and answers about which brain tumors are counted. CBS12 News has covered families’ concerns for well over a decade. The analysis covers diagnoses through 2023, leaving more recent cases outside its scope. It also documents a change in the tumor classifications included compared with the state’s 2019 review. Lucie County Health Officer Clint Sperber directed the I-Team to the report, accompanying resources and a scientific journal article addressing environmental risk factors. hero.body:
Florida health officials released an updated brain cancer review Thursday that found no statistically significant excess of glioblastoma in St. Lucie County or the three ZIP codes examined. The assessment covers diagnoses from 2014 through 2023 in St. Lucie, Martin and Indian River counties. Its scope is limited to glioblastoma, with other tumor types, diagnoses after 2023 and street-level patterns falling outside the analysis. Families tracking brain tumor diagnoses in Fort Pierce continue to seek a closer examination of patients who lived near one another.

In St. Lucie County, officials recorded 95 glioblastoma diagnoses from 2019 through 2023, compared with approximately 92 expected. Across the full decade, ZIP code 34952 had 32 diagnoses, compared with approximately 26 expected; 34983 had 21, compared with approximately 20 expected; and 34982 had 12, compared with approximately 13 expected. The state compared recorded diagnoses with expectations based on statewide cancer rates, accounting for age. Officials said small case counts can fluctuate by chance, while population growth can increase diagnoses without increasing underlying risk. The accompanying FAQ identifies 2023 as the latest finalized cancer registry year, with reporting time allowing checks for completeness and accuracy.

Stephanie Ankiel, with the Brain Cancer Foundation of the Treasure Coast, wants officials to examine individual streets. The department said evolving medical classifications placed oligodendroglioma codes 9450 and 9451, which were included in its 2019 analysis, outside the current glioblastoma definition. The Florida Cancer Data System generally records patients’ addresses at diagnosis, which may differ from where they lived years earlier or experienced a potentially relevant exposure. The registry’s residential-history and environmental-exposure limitations also constrain the review. hero.headline: Martin County judge gives Daniel Warren effective life sentence in AI child pornography case
hero.body:
A Martin County judge sentenced Daniel Warren to the equivalent of life in prison for using artificial intelligence to create child pornography in a case involving covert photographs of neighborhood children.

Judge Elizabeth Metzger imposed just over 1,000 months per count, the minimum allowable sentence under the law, after deciding a lesser sentence was not appropriate. Warren was charged with 75 felony counts of possession of child pornography and seven felony counts of video voyeurism.

Prosecutor Kristen Chase said Warren secretly photographed children whose parents trusted him, then used AI to turn those photographs into sexualized images that he shared with others.

“His innocent neighbors, whose parents trusted him to be appropriate with their children, he was taking covert photos of them and then asking for those children to be transformed into some sexualized image which he shared with others,” Chase said.

Warren was arrested in 2024. The Martin County Sheriff's Office said at the time that it was the agency's first case involving AI and child exploitation.

A man who identified himself as an extended family member testified before the judge Wednesday. “That would be a detriment to the children to have this man even anywhere near a child,” he said.

Before sentencing, Warren spoke about the damage to his relationships. “My entire community, [I] basically destroyed every friendship I've built,” he said. “I dwell on it every night.” When his defense attorney asked whether he dwells on the decisions he made, Warren answered, “Absolutely.”

hero.headline: Some Florida ACA customers auto-enrolled in replacement health plans for 2027
hero.body:
Some Florida customers who buy health insurance through the Affordable Care Act marketplace are being automatically enrolled in replacement plans for 2027 without realizing it. With open enrollment beginning Nov. 1, a Florida health advocate is urging customers to review their options and check coverage for their doctors and medications.

Melissa Smith, of West Palm Beach, knew she would need to find a new plan because her current insurer was leaving the program at the end of the year. She learned she had been automatically enrolled in another plan when a different insurance company began contacting her.

“All of a sudden I started getting phone calls, text messages, and emails from another health insurance company saying congrats, you're enrolled, and then getting a bill from them,” Smith said. She later determined that her doctor was outside the new plan's network and said she did not want that plan.

Scott Darius of Florida Voices for Health said the marketplace uses automatic re-enrollment for existing customers. “If your plan has changed or disappeared, the marketplace will often put you in a plan that they deem to be similar,” he said.

Darius said most plans have already posted their 2027 rates, with rates overall up about 10%. He recommends starting the enrollment process by finding someone trustworthy to help review the choices. Enrollment can be completed at healthcare.gov.

Before choosing a plan, Darius advises customers to make a list of priorities, including doctors they want to keep seeing and medications they need covered. He recommends working with a trusted source to compare the options against that list.

hero.headline: Martin County judge imposes effective life sentence in AI child exploitation case
hero.body:
Martin County Judge Elizabeth Metzger imposed a prison sentence effectively equal to life on Daniel Warren for using artificial intelligence to create child sexual abuse material. Warren used covert photos of neighborhood children to generate sexualized images that he shared with others, prosecutor Kristen Chase said.

Metzger imposed the minimum allowable sentence under the law, just over 1,000 months per count, after deciding a lesser sentence was not appropriate. Warren was arrested in 2024 and charged with 75 felony counts of possession of child pornography and seven felony counts of video voyeurism. At the time of his arrest, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said it was its first case involving AI and child exploitation.

Chase said the children were Warren's neighbors and their parents had trusted him to behave appropriately around them. A man who identified himself as an extended family member testified before the judge Wednesday. "That would be a detriment to the children to have this man even anywhere near a child," he said.

Before sentencing, Warren expressed remorse and said he had destroyed friendships throughout his community. "I dwell on it every night," Warren said. When his defense attorney asked whether he dwells on the decisions he made, Warren answered, "Absolutely."

hero.headline: Manatee rescued from shallow Indian River County ditch and safely released
hero.body:
A manatee found stranded in a shallow ditch in Indian River County was rescued Tuesday and later released elsewhere in the county, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. Deputies assisted the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission’s manatee rescue team with the effort to move the animal out of the ditch. The Sheriff’s Office said the manatee was transported safely to an area suitable for its release. The rescue and relocation took place within Indian River County, where the animal had been found stranded. Photos and video shared by the Sheriff’s Office show crews working at the ditch.

The response brought together sheriff’s deputies and the state agency’s team that handles manatee rescues. According to the Sheriff’s Office, deputies helped the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission team safely relocate the stranded animal on Tuesday. The manatee was in a shallow ditch when crews worked to rescue it, as seen in the images released by the agency. The Sheriff’s Office described its deputies’ role as assisting the FWC team with the relocation. Their involvement was part of the effort to get the manatee out of the place where it had become stranded and move it to a suitable release area.

After the rescue from the ditch, the manatee was safely transported for release, the Sheriff’s Office said. The destination was another area within Indian River County that was suitable for the animal. The relocation therefore kept the manatee in the same county while moving it away from the shallow ditch where it had been found. The Sheriff’s Office reported that the transport and release were completed safely. That release was the outcome of the response involving deputies and the FWC manatee rescue team, which had worked to relocate the animal after it was discovered stranded in the ditch.

The Sheriff’s Office also shared a visual account of the rescue through video and photographs showing crews at work. Those images document the effort to rescue the manatee from the shallow ditch, while the agency’s account confirms that the animal was subsequently transported and released. Both the rescue location and the release area were in Indian River County, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The Tuesday response ended with the manatee safely released in a suitable area following the rescue team’s work and the assistance provided by sheriff’s deputies.

hero.headline: Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicates Fort Pierce center with larger kitchen, food storage
hero.body:
The Treasure Coast Food Bank dedicated its new 132,000-square-foot regional operations center in Fort Pierce Thursday morning, bringing its work under one roof and expanding food storage and meal preparation capacity. The facility at 401 Loop Road includes a production kitchen capable of producing up to 25,000 meals a day during a disaster. It also supports fresh food programs, nutrition education, benefits assistance and workforce training.

The production kitchen more than doubled in size, growing from 7,000 to 15,000 square feet. Along with its disaster-response capacity, the kitchen prepares nutritious meals for the community. The new freezer area alone could fit one and a half of the food bank’s former facilities. Founded in 1988, the organization is the only food bank serving Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties. It reaches about 250,000 people each week and works with hundreds of nonprofit partners.

The center is designed to meet immediate needs and help people build stability for the future. Adults and children can take nutrition education classes on site, while seniors receive nutrition information with delivered food boxes. Three job-training programs focus on culinary, hospitality and barista skills. Students learn skills including knife safety, food safety and making pasta from scratch. The programs offer certifications in stages, and some courses are free.

During Thursday’s dedication, 10 community members participated in a ceremonial First Box packing representing the network behind the food bank’s work. Robin Safley of Feeding Florida added fresh vegetables on behalf of the statewide hunger-relief network. Donor Dee Locke added fresh fruit, and volunteer Tatiana Rousseau added peanut butter. The food bank’s capital campaign is continuing, with donations accepted through the Feed Unite Flourish capital campaign page.

hero.headline: Viewing in Fort Pierce, memorial in Port St. Lucie announced for firefighter Austin Hodge
hero.body:
A public viewing in Fort Pierce and a memorial service in Port St. Lucie have been announced for St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died in the line of duty Oct. 24. The district coordinated the arrangements with Hodge's family and Stone Brothers Funeral Home.

The public viewing will be held at River of Life Fellowship Church, located at 3950 Juanita Avenue in Fort Pierce. A memorial service will follow at Christ Fellowship Church, located at 10250 SW Village Parkway in Port St. Lucie.

Hodge served the St. Lucie County community for more than nine years, according to the fire district. “The St. Lucie County Fire District continues to mourn the loss of Firefighter/Paramedic Austin Hodge,” the agency said in a statement. “His loss is deeply felt by his family, friends, fellow firefighters, and the many lives he touched throughout his years of service.”

The district thanked the community for supporting Hodge's family and fellow firefighters following his death. “We remain grateful for the outpouring of love and support extended to Austin's family and our Fire District family during this difficult time,” the agency said.

hero.headline: Florida student aid breach may have exposed Social Security numbers of 4.9 million people
hero.body:
Unauthorized access to Florida’s student financial aid website may have exposed personal information, including Social Security numbers, belonging to approximately 4.9 million people, the Florida Department of Education said Thursday. Department staff became aware of the unauthorized access on Oct. 19. Officials believe the breach was limited to the Florida Student Financial Aid website.

The department recommends that people monitor their financial and online accounts for suspicious activity and regularly review account statements and credit reports. It also recommends considering a fraud alert or credit freeze with the major credit bureaus. Consumers can obtain free credit reports through AnnualCreditReport.com. The Federal Trade Commission’s IdentityTheft.gov website offers additional information about responding to a data breach.

Current financial aid is not at risk, and the incident will not delay financial aid disbursements or tuition payments from the department, officials said. The breach also will not affect eligibility for scholarships, grants or student loans from the department. Some department websites and online services may experience temporary disruptions while officials work to restore full functionality.

The department said it activated its cybersecurity response protocols after detecting the incident, took steps to contain the unauthorized activity and secure its systems, and notified the Florida Attorney General’s Office. It is working with the Florida Digital Service and the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. The unauthorized access remains under criminal investigation.

Anyone with questions about the breach can contact the department at databreach@fldoe.org. The department is posting updates on its data breach information page and said information could change as the criminal investigation continues.

hero.headline: State review finds St. Lucie County glioblastoma cases in line with expectations
hero.body:
An updated Florida Department of Health review of concerns about a possible glioblastoma cluster in St. Lucie County found 95 cases from 2019 through 2023, compared with 92 expected. Health officials say the difference is not statistically significant. The countywide analysis does not examine concentrations on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods, leaving families’ concerns about geographic patterns unresolved.

The findings largely match those of the state’s original 2019 report, which found that the number of cases did not warrant a more intensive investigation. Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, said the latest review reached the same conclusion about expected cases. The review also considered existing water and radiation monitoring records. Unlike the 2019 report, the updated analysis did not break down cases by age or sex because officials said there were too few cases to make those comparisons statistically reliable.

Families’ concerns have centered partly on where patients lived. Some patients lived within blocks of one another, others on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home. Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns. Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, but some of the local patients were in their 30s, and Kyle Vericella was 18. Sperber acknowledged that the updated analysis does not closely examine whether patients lived near one another on particular streets or within specific neighborhoods.

Deb Johnston wants investigators to look more closely at individual neighborhoods, particularly the White City area. Her son, Lenny Schelin Jr., died at 33, just 17 months after his glioblastoma diagnosis. Nearly eight years after his death, Johnston remains grateful that officials continue to review the cases, but she wants a closer examination of the geographic patterns. “I haven't given up; it's just you get tired,” she said.

The Florida Department of Health has invested at least $9 million in glioblastoma research since concerns about local cases drew attention. Johnston also supports research through an annual fishing tournament honoring her son, who loved fishing. The event has raised nearly $300,000 for glioblastoma research, and another tournament is approaching.
hero.article_text: Nearly eight years after WPTV first investigated concerns about a possible cluster of glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County, health officials have reviewed the numbers again.The latest findings show the number of cases remains in line with what would be expected based on the county's population, but families who lost loved ones to the deadly brain cancer say important questions remain unanswered.WATCH THE REPORT BELOW: The latest review by the Florida Department of Health follows years of WPTV reporting into concerns raised by patients and families who discovered they lived near others diagnosed with the same aggressive form of brain cancer.While health officials say the data does not show a statistically significant increase in cases, the review does not examine whether patients were concentrated on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods.For families who have spent years searching for answers, that distinction matters.READ THE FULL STATE REPORT BELOW: A young man's death helped spark an investigationFor Deb Johnston, the loss of her son, Lenny Schelin Jr., is still painful."It's been eight years since Lenny passed," she said.Lenny was just 33 years old when he died from glioblastoma, one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer.He was healthy, active and loved fishing. He survived just 17 months after his diagnosis."Everybody loved Lenny. He just had this charm about him," his mother recalled.Lenny's story was among the first that helped WPTV uncover concerns about glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Other patients included Mark Cunningham, who was also in his 30s, and Kyle Vericella, who was just 18.After WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts uncovered the local cases, dozens of additional patients and family members contacted her with their stories.Area doctors and neurosurgeons also expressed concerns.Glioblastoma is most commonly diagnosed in older adults, making the younger ages of some patients particularly troubling to their families.But it wasn't just their ages that raised questions.As patients began connecting with one another, WPTV mapped where they lived beginning in 2018.Some lived within blocks of one another. Others lived on the same street. In one case, unrelated patients had lived in the same home.The reporting drew attention from lawmakers, environmental advocate Erin Brockovich and the Florida Department of Health.What did the original 2019 investigation find?The concerns prompted health officials to examine glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County."You brought it to my attention. It was alarming; it was nerve-wracking," Clint Sperber, administrator for the Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County, told WPTV's Meghan McRoberts.Sperber said the concerns led to a request for assistance from Florida's cancer registry."I asked for assistance from our cancer registry through our leadership, my boss," he said. "And we were able to help collect a lot of information."That information was compiled into a report released in 2019.Despite concerns about the number of patients diagnosed with glioblastoma, the report did not find a statistically significant increase in cases that would warrant a more intensive investigation.Health officials also reviewed existing environmental monitoring information, including public water utility data and radiation monitoring records associated with the area's power plant.Sperber pointed to ongoing environmental monitoring as part of the state's assessment."There is water testing, there is vegetation testing, they look at watermelon, milk, fish, soil, they would know if there is any release of radiation," Sperber said.The findings were disappointing for families who had hoped the investigation would uncover an explanation."I was like deflated because we worked so hard," Johnston said.What does the latest glioblastoma review show?Seven years after the original report, health officials have taken another look at glioblastoma cases in St. Lucie County.Their conclusion remains largely unchanged."The conclusion that was found in 2019 is the same one we have today," Sperber told WPTV. hero.headline: Erosion hits Ocean Drive beachfront parking in Vero Beach as king tides persist
hero.body:
Coastal erosion caused by king tides and strong onshore winds has affected a section of beachfront parking on Ocean Drive in Vero Beach, prompting officials to contact park officials about public safety measures. The area is one of the erosion hot spots officials have identified along the coast.

Quintin Bergman, the resource manager with Indian River County, is monitoring the damage along the Vero Beach boardwalk. He said the erosion is approaching severe as the two weather events continue to affect the shoreline. “I would classify this as leaning more on the severe side of erosion. It's not extreme by any means, but definitely we are very concerned,” Bergman said.

The forecast calls for elevated winds for a few more days, and king tides will continue to affect the water level, Bergman said. “We're still in the middle of this. We're not through with the weather event. The forecast is showing elevated winds for a few more days, and the king tide event is still going to be affecting the tide.” Officials plan to assess the damage after the weather event passes.

Beachgoers have also noticed changes to the shoreline. Svetlana Ryan was among those still enjoying the view in Vero Beach despite the erosion. “We noticed because there was so much sand before, and now it's just a wall. But you do with whatever you have to do here in Vero Beach,” Ryan said.

hero.headline: Murray Middle School breaks ground on $33 million rebuild after tornado damage
hero.body:
Murray Middle School has broken ground on a $33 million rebuilding phase that will add permanent learning and performing arts spaces after a tornado spawned by Hurricane Milton damaged three main buildings and forced students into portable classrooms. School officials expect gym renovations to be completed by August 2027 and the new buildings to be finished by December 2027.

Students and staff gathered for the groundbreaking as the school moves into the second phase of its campus rebuilding project. The work includes a performing arts wing with band and choir rooms, new learning spaces and gym renovations. Murray Middle School Principal Tiffany Roth said students will also have a new media center, an art room and an agriculture room.

Martin County Superintendent Michael Maine said campus improvements were planned before Hurricane Milton, but the storm damage added urgency. About $33 million has been approved for the second phase, according to school officials. “When Hurricane Milton came through and spawned the tornado, it took down three of our main buildings that we rely on every single day,” Maine said. “We couldn't have our students displaced in portables any longer than we needed to.”

Choir was among the programs forced out of permanent space by the storm. Dr. Anita Caswell, Murray Middle School's choir and drama director, said the damage destroyed decades of program materials, including costumes and props. “It was 60 years of drama props,” Caswell said. “Our dresses were in that, the boys' vest that we used to sing in, and just to see it all mangled and stuck up on the wall, it just hurt.”

Caswell said students continued singing in a portable classroom and earned straight superior ratings that year. Murray Middle student Nicholas Lowe said the move required him to adjust to a different learning environment. Roth said she hopes students take pride in being Murray Lions and enjoy the new buildings when they are finished.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective charged with DUI after Vero Beach crash, put on unpaid leave
hero.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff's detective Tyler Horstman has been charged with DUI and placed on unpaid administrative leave following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that seriously injured a woman and hospitalized her son. Investigators said Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with their SUV.

The crash happened at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. Investigators said the SUV's driver ran a red light while Horstman had a green light. All three people were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit.

Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. During his assessment, Horstman said he had consumed "a few beers" earlier in the evening, according to the affidavit. Police said the agency truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash.

Horstman turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail on Monday. Police said the investigation took several months and involved search warrants, subpoenas and obtaining records. He faces several charges, including DUI. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Horstman was placed on unpaid administrative leave in accordance with agency policy.

"Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process," Del Toro said in a statement.

hero.headline: Mattamy Homes transferring 125 acres in Martin County for St. Lucie River muck storage
hero.body:
Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County to store muck dredged from the St. Lucie River as part of efforts to improve water quality. The removal project will begin once federal funding is authorized, a company official said.

The parcel is in the northern section of the Newfield development. The developer said the land was donated to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, a federal plan to restore, protect and preserve South Florida's water resources.

James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres. Together, the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck removed from the river, Fitzgerald said.

Fitzgerald said the muck will dry out after removal. He expressed hope that the land could eventually be used for recreation or, depending on the county's needs, other environmental restoration projects.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested, accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger
cards.teaser: Investigators say Anthony Pizzarelli demanded an apology and support for government audits, including in St. Lucie County. He denied using his communications as leverage.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he tried to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger by threatening lawsuits and ethics complaints unless she publicly apologized and supported government audits, including in St. Lucie County. The allegations against Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, are outlined in a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office probable cause affidavit.

Pizzarelli faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. He told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he wanted an apology over an incident involving an email on which she had been copied and was seeking her support for his complaints. He is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9, offering to leave her out of planned lawsuits and ethics complaints if she issued a swift public apology. He proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, he wanted audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and investigations into government contracting.

The affidavit says Pizzarelli sent a voice memo directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone on May 18, 2026. Among his statements were “I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice,” and “you don't know what I can do.” Weinberger told investigators she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family's safety. A first-term Republican, she represents Florida House District 94, which is entirely within Palm Beach County.

In 2025, Pizzarelli was arrested after being accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies said the communications escalated in tone and content, raising concern among officials. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from that case had been dropped.

Weinberger's campaign also faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election involving Nicholas Farley, not Pizzarelli. Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library.

hero.headline: Murray Middle School breaks ground on $33 million rebuilding phase
hero.body:
Murray Middle School has broken ground on a $33 million rebuilding phase that will replace storm-damaged spaces and move displaced students and programs out of portable classrooms, according to Martin County school officials. The project follows damage to three main buildings from a tornado spawned by Hurricane Milton.

School officials said about $33 million has been approved for the second phase of the campus project. The work includes new learning spaces, a performing arts wing and renovations to the gym. The gym is expected to be completed by August 2027, with the new buildings expected to be finished by December 2027. Principal Tiffany Roth said the project includes a media center, an art room and an agriculture room, along with rooms for band and choir in the performing arts wing.

Students and staff gathered for the groundbreaking as rebuilding continued. Martin County Superintendent Michael Maine said improvements to Murray Middle School were planned before Hurricane Milton, but the tornado damage made the work more urgent. “When Hurricane Milton came through and spawned the tornado, it took down three of our main buildings that we rely on every single day,” Maine said. “We couldn't have our students displaced in portables any longer than we needed to.”

Choir was among the programs displaced by the storm. Dr. Anita Caswell, Murray Middle School's choir and drama director, said the storm destroyed decades of program materials, including costumes and drama props. “It was 60 years of drama props,” Caswell said. Her students continued singing in a portable classroom, and she said the choir earned straight superior ratings that year.

For student Nicholas Lowe, the move meant adjusting to a different learning environment. “It was a big change, but also I had to adapt to it to, like, be better for the choir,” Lowe said. Roth said she hopes the completed campus will give students a renewed sense of pride in being Murray Lions.

cards.headline: Siblings seek answers after St. Lucie County firefighter found unresponsive in bunk
cards.teaser: Austin Hodge’s siblings say the firefighter-paramedic appeared normal hours before he was found unresponsive at the firehouse. They are seeking answers about his death.
cards.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died on duty Oct. 24, say the 34-year-old was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk early that morning. They are seeking answers about his final hours, and his family says they do not yet know what caused his death. His sister, Alexis Hodge, said relatives were told he had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis and her brother, Javan Hodge, gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. In addition to his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, his family said.

Javan said the family wants to understand the events leading to Austin’s death. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” he said. Alexis said relatives want to know who was around Austin and who saw him before he was found unresponsive. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Austin’s death comes just over a year after the death of his 26-year-old brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, who also served with the fire district. The family said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. Relatives raised concerns about the medical care Jairus received, and Austin sought answers and advocated for his brother. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said.

Alexis and Javan said they intend to carry on both brothers’ legacy. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a career in healthcare. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said. “The love I have for them is unimaginable. It has no bounds.”

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective accused of speeding in Vero Beach DUI crash
hero.teaser: An arrest report says the woman in the other vehicle suffered a traumatic brain injury. The Sheriff’s Office has put its internal investigation on hold pending the criminal case.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Detective Tyler Horstman is accused of driving 63 mph in a 35 mph zone before a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that left another driver with a traumatic brain injury. The allegations are detailed in an arrest report tied to the felony DUI case against Horstman, who turned himself in Monday afternoon after a warrant was issued.

The crash happened about 11:25 p.m. at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. According to the arrest report, Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he struck a Chevy Equinox carrying a woman and an infant. Vero Beach police say Horstman entered the intersection on a green light and the other driver entered against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital. The report describes the woman’s injury as “a traumatic brain injury” and says the infant was alert and responsive.

The arrest report says Horstman acknowledged having a few beers earlier in the evening. It describes a “faint odor of alcohol on his breath” and says he was “lethargic and dazed” and “drowsy and periodically dozing off.” Blood-test results showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit, according to the Sheriff’s Office.

The Sheriff’s Office received those results September 9, and Horstman was placed on administrative leave September 15. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation.

The felony warrant issued Monday lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9.

On September 9, the Sheriff’s Office received Horstman’s blood-test results. They showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit. According to the arrest report, March 1 at about 11:25pm at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach, Horstman was off-duty driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he hit a Chevy Equinox with a woman and an infant inside. Vero Beach police say Horstman was driving at 63 mph in a posted 35 mph zone and entered the intersection on a green light. The other driver entered the intersection against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital, and the infant was not injured. The arrest report says: "Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening." It says Horstman had a "faint odor of alcohol on his breath" and it says Horstman was "lethargic and dazed" and that he was "drowsy and periodically dozing off." The woman in the vehicle he hit suffered "a traumatic brain injury" and the infant was alert and responsive. The arrest report says Horstman had a blood-alcohol level of .246, which is three times the legal limit at which a person is considered too impaired to drive in Florida. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15, according to the St. A felony arrest warrant was issued Monday. It lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. The crash happened in March, but Horstman was not arrested until late October. "It's very typical in cases like this take months and months, and it's very frustrating for victims and their families, and also for the public, who are waiting for justice," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. He is now an attorney in private practice in West Palm Beach. cards.headline: Siblings seek answers after St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge’s death
cards.teaser: Austin Hodge’s siblings say the family was told he was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk. They are seeking answers about his final hours and what caused his death.
cards.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge are seeking answers about his death after the 34-year-old died while on duty Oct. 24. His siblings, Alexis Hodge and Javan Hodge, want to understand what happened in his final hours and what caused his death.

Alexis said the family was told Austin appeared to be himself before going to bed. He had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes, according to the account relayed to them. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis and Javan gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, his family said.

Austin’s death came just over a year after the death of his younger brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, 26, who also served with the fire district. The family said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. They raised concerns about the medical care Jairus received and said Austin sought answers and advocated for his brother. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said. “He would not rest until he could spread Jay’s legacy globally.”

Now, Alexis and Javan are seeking answers about Austin. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. Alexis said they want to establish who was around Austin and who saw him before he was found unresponsive. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Both siblings said they are determined to make Austin and Jairus proud. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a career in healthcare. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said. “The love I have for them is unimaginable. It has no bounds.”

hero.headline: Kanner Highway data center exempt from Martin County's one-year application pause
hero.body:
The Florida Gateway Project, a proposed data center off Kanner Highway, remains exempt from the one-year pause on large-scale data center applications that Martin County commissioners unanimously approved at a second public hearing. County staff expect the proposal’s development review to take a year, even as the moratorium pauses other applications.

The Florida Gateway Project application was submitted Oct. 12, one day before commissioners held the first public hearing on the moratorium. The county attorney said the information arrived late the day before that hearing and that commissioners were alerted as soon as possible. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed during the second hearing that the county had received a data center application on Kanner Highway. The proposal will proceed through the county’s development review process.

The moratorium gives staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. Every resident who spoke during public comment at the second hearing opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades, called for further study. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," Darling said.

A resident who said they live one mile from the proposed Florida Gateway Project raised concerns about its scale, electricity demand and potential water use. Resident Richard Miller also objected to locating data centers near people’s homes. "These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," Miller said.
hero.article_text: Martin County commissioners unanimously voted during a second public hearing to implement a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center applications, giving staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. During the hearing, every resident who spoke during public comment opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," said Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades. "I don’t want to spend another year or longer where somebody that I know is trying to do me great bodily harm. Folks, it’s in your hands. These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," said resident Richard Miller. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed there is an applicant for a data center. "One of them is the Florida Gateway Project, where this one project has been ... a data center application has come on Kanner Highway," Capps said. A resident who lives near the proposed site raised concerns about the scale of the project. "I happen to live one mile from this new proposed mega center, 100 MW, and 100 MW is like unbelievable to power 100,000 homes, and that's going to be a mile from me. Who knows how much water it's going to use," the resident said. Commissioner Vargas expressed frustration with the application process. "I was not too happy about hearing this application. I even requested the receipt, which I have here in my hand, and the date ... We should give them back and say they don't want you here. It's okay, you go elsewhere," Vargas said. The application for the Florida Gateway Project was submitted on Oct. 12, with the first public hearing held the following day. "We got the information late on the Monday before the 13th ... so, I didn't have the information in advance of the 13th. At the meeting on the 13th, I disclosed to everybody that I had just found out about it. I'm sorry, Commissioner, we did alert the commission as soon as we could," said County Attorney Elysse A. "I understand, but somebody took the money on this date is what I'm trying to say. Doesn't anybody talk to anybody here?" Vargas said. The application will go through the development review process, which staff said is expected to take a year. Aside from this application, there are currently no other large-scale data center applications pending. St. Lucie County sheriff’s deputy Tyler Horstman, arrested Monday on a felony DUI charge tied to a March 1 crash in Vero Beach, was driving 63 mph in a 35 mph zone and had a blood-alcohol level of 0.246, according to police and his arrest report. The woman driving the other vehicle suffered a traumatic brain injury, the report says. Horstman turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office.

The crash happened about 11:25 p.m. at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he struck a Chevy Equinox carrying the woman and an infant, according to the arrest report. Vero Beach police said Horstman entered the intersection on a green light and the other driver entered against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital. The infant was alert and responsive, according to the report.

The arrest report says Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening. It describes a “faint odor of alcohol on his breath” and says he was “lethargic and dazed” and “drowsy and periodically dozing off.” The Sheriff’s Office received his blood-test results on September 9. His blood-alcohol concentration of 0.246 was more than three times Florida’s legal limit. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15.

The felony warrant issued Monday lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective charged with DUI, put on unpaid leave after Vero Beach crash
hero.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff’s detective Tyler Horstman has been charged with DUI and placed on unpaid administrative leave following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that seriously injured a woman and hospitalized her son. Investigators said Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with an SUV at Beachland Boulevard and A1A.

Police said the truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash. Investigators determined that the SUV’s driver ran a red light and that Horstman had a green light. All three people involved were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. Police said the crash could have been fatal.

Investigators determined that Horstman’s blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, he said during his assessment that he had consumed “a few beers” earlier in the evening. Horstman turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail on Monday. Police said the investigation took several months and involved search warrants, subpoenas and obtaining records. He faces several charges, including DUI.

St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Horstman was placed on unpaid administrative leave in accordance with agency policy. “Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process,” Del Toro said. “The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires.”

cards.headline: Family seeks answers in St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge’s death
cards.teaser: Austin Hodge’s siblings say the 34-year-old was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk after appearing normal hours earlier. They are seeking answers about his final hours.
cards.body:
The family of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died while on duty Oct. 24, says he was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk early that morning and taken to a hospital. His siblings are seeking answers about his final hours and say they do not yet know what caused the 34-year-old’s death.

His sister, Alexis Hodge, said the family was told Austin had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis and her brother, Javan Hodge, gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. In addition to working as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family. “It’s a shock to literally all of us,” Alexis said. “Nobody knows what happened.”

Austin’s death came just over a year after the death of his younger brother, 26-year-old Jairus “Jay” Hodge, who also served with the fire district. The family said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. They said concerns about the medical care Jairus received led Austin to seek answers and advocate for his brother. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said. “He would not rest until he could spread Jay’s legacy globally.”

Now, Alexis and Javan want to understand what happened to Austin before he was found unresponsive, including who was around him and who saw him. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. Alexis said getting answers is important to her grieving process. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Both siblings said they are determined to make Austin and Jairus proud. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a healthcare career. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective charged with DUI, put on unpaid leave after Vero Beach crash
hero.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff's detective Tyler Horstman faces charges including DUI and has been placed on unpaid administrative leave following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that seriously injured a woman and hospitalized her son. Police said the unmarked agency pickup truck Horstman was driving was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the collision.

The crash happened at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A while Horstman was off duty. Investigators said the driver of the SUV carrying the woman and her son ran a red light, while Horstman had a green light. All three people were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. Police said the crash could have been fatal.

Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, he said during his assessment that he had consumed “a few beers” earlier in the evening. Police said the investigation took several months as investigators worked through search warrants, subpoenas and records. Horstman turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail on Monday. His unpaid administrative leave is in accordance with agency policy, according to St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro.

“Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process,” Del Toro said in a statement. “The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires.”

cards.headline: Indian River County sets record with 14,083 turtle nests as rough surf threatens eggs
cards.teaser: Decades of conservation helped Indian River County reach its highest nest count. Rough surf and king tides now threaten remaining nests and have delayed damage surveys.
cards.body:
Indian River County recorded a record 14,083 sea turtle nests as of Oct. 22, while rough surf and king tides threaten remaining nests and have delayed surveys to assess damage. The total surpassed the county’s previous record, set in 2023, by approximately 2,000 nests, according to Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen. Loggerheads accounted for 10,045 nests, followed by 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. Whalen said loggerheads drove much of the increase that pushed the county to its highest recorded total.

Whalen credited decades of conservation work for the milestone, including monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and efforts to encourage turtle-friendly beach practices. Along the county’s 22.4-mile coastline, orange markers identify approximately one in 10 nests. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. The markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity. Whalen said marking all 14,000 nests would leave beachgoers little room to sit. The long-term gains reflect years of work protecting both sea turtles and their nesting beaches, he said.

A nor’easter and king tides have brought powerful waves and high water as nesting season winds down. Waves strip sand from the beach, potentially exposing buried eggs, and unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween, though some nests may continue incubating beyond that date.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission advises beachgoers to leave exposed eggs in place rather than collect or rebury them. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive. Storm currents can also carry young turtles ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. People should not pick them up or return them to the ocean, but should immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance. Beachgoers can help keep nesting beaches clean, flat and dark by removing beach gear, filling holes, flattening sandcastles and keeping lights off the beach at night.
cards.article_text: Indian River County’s sea turtles broke a record. The county documented 14,083 nests as of Thursday, its highest total ever recorded. Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen credits decades of conservation efforts for the milestone. This is actually a really big deal because what we’re seeing is decades of conservation paying off, Whalen said. But the record season is facing a rough finish. Powerful waves and high tides are eroding beaches, threatening some remaining nests. Loggerheads lead the record season The county’s latest dashboard lists 10,045 loggerhead nests, 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. The total surpassed the previous record, set in 2023, by approximately 2,000 nests, according to Whalen. Loggerheads drove much of that increase. They’re dominating with 10,000 nests across our entire coastline, which is an insane number, Whalen said. The orange markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity. The county marks approximately one in 10 nests along its 22.4-mile coastline. If we mark 14,000 nests you wouldn’t have anywhere to sit on the beach, Whalen said. And like seriously it would be a sea of orange. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. Whalen said the long-term gains reflect years of work protecting turtles and their nesting beaches. Those efforts include monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and encouraging turtle-friendly beach practices. Rough surf threatens remaining nests A nor’easter and king tides have brought challenging conditions as nesting season winds down. Waves strip away sand, potentially exposing eggs buried beneath the beach. Unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. A lot of them have already hatched out, a lot of them have made it to the water safely, Whalen said. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween. Some nests may continue incubating beyond that date. Nesting numbers across the Treasure Coast Other counties also provided nesting figures. The totals cover different reporting dates and monitoring areas. Indian River County : As of Oct. 22, the county recorded 14,083 nests: 10,045 loggerhead, 3,970 green turtle and 68 leatherback nests. Lucie County : As of Sept. 30, the county recorded 10,239 nests: 9,111 loggerhead, 956 green turtle and 172 leatherback nests. Martin County: As of Sept. 28, its Hutchinson Island monitoring area recorded 4,874 nests: 4,532 loggerhead, 161 green turtle and 181 leatherback nests. Martin County’s figures cover approximately 7.5 miles of Hutchinson Island shoreline. That area stretches from the north side of St. Lucie Inlet to the Martin St. CBS12 News has requested Palm Beach County’s latest countywide figures from FWC and is awaiting those numbers. Boca Raton sees high nest counts, lower hatch success In Boca Raton, a strong nesting season did not translate into equally strong hatching results. David Anderson, sea turtle conservation coordinator at Gumbo Limbo Nature Center, reported the city’s third-highest nesting season. That included record counts of 1,118 loggerhead nests and 43 leatherback nests. But an average of only about 50% of the eggs in inventoried nests hatched. Anderson said a typical hatch rate would be 70% to 80% or more. He attributed some losses to prolonged hot, dry conditions during peak incubation. High sand temperatures can prevent embryos from continuing to develop. Storms and high tides also washed out approximately 185 nests, Anderson said. Predators affected another 13 nests. Artificial lighting created additional problems after hatching. Anderson said hatchlings from at least 85 nests became disoriented and headed into the dunes. Staff plan to evaluate beachfront lighting and work with nearby properties before next season. So sure, it’s sad to see so many hatchlings and eggs not fully developed, but once again, we had a great nesting season, Anderson said. So as long as the nesting numbers continue to climb, it gives us hope. What to do if you find eggs or hatchlings The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission says sea turtles spread their nests across the season. That strategy helps some nests survive even when storms damage others. After rough weather, beachgoers may find exposed eggs or young turtles washed ashore. FWC says to leave exposed eggs in place. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive, and people should not collect or rebury them. Storm currents can also carry young turtles back ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. Do not pick them up or return them to the ocean. Instead, immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance, according to FWC. Beachgoers can help by keeping beaches clean, flat and dark. Remove beach gear, fill holes, flatten sandcastles and keep lights off the beach at night.

The sheriff's office also reported flooding affecting SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. Residents are being urged to stay away from the affected areas and to exercise extreme caution. The warning includes a reminder not to try to drive through flooded roads. Anyone who needs emergency assistance should call 911, the sheriff's office said in its notice about the flooding in Palm City.

The sheriff's office described the flooding along SW Dyer Point Road as significant and said the road cannot be passed. SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue are also among the locations affected by the flooding, according to the agency. Its warning to residents is to avoid these areas rather than attempt to travel through the floodwater. The notice identifies SW Dyer Point Road as impassable and names the other two streets as additional places experiencing flooding. For anyone considering driving in the affected areas, the sheriff's office's instruction is clear: Do not attempt to drive through a flooded roadway.

High-water rescue vehicles are being deployed to assist people who become stranded, whether they are in a vehicle or in a home, the sheriff's office said. The deployment is intended to help people in either situation as flooding affects the Palm City streets. The agency's notice pairs the rescue deployment with its request that residents avoid the flooded areas. People should not try to drive through the water, even as rescue vehicles are being sent to assist those who are stranded. The sheriff's office is urging extreme caution around the affected locations and directing anyone needing emergency assistance to call 911.
