hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective charged with DUI after Vero Beach crash
hero.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff's detective Tyler Horstman has been charged with DUI following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that seriously injured a woman and hospitalized her son. Investigators said Horstman was driving an unmarked agency pickup truck at about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the collision.

Horstman was off duty when the truck collided with an SUV carrying the woman and her son at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. Investigators determined that the SUV's driver ran a red light and Horstman had a green light. Separately, investigators found that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, he said during his assessment that he had consumed “a few beers” earlier in the evening.

All three people involved in the crash were hospitalized. The child was later released, but the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. Police said the crash could have been fatal.

Horstman turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail on Monday and was placed on unpaid administrative leave in accordance with agency policy. Police said the investigation took several months as investigators worked through search warrants, subpoenas and records.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said employees accused of violating the law must be held accountable through the appropriate process. “The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires.”

hero.headline: Indian River County records 14,083 sea turtle nests as rough surf threatens season’s end
hero.body:
Indian River County recorded a historic 14,083 sea turtle nests as of Oct. 22, roughly 2,000 more than its previous record in 2023. Rough surf and king tides are threatening some remaining nests, while unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage.

The county’s latest dashboard lists 10,045 loggerhead nests, 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen said loggerheads drove much of the increase and credited decades of conservation efforts for the milestone. Those efforts include monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and encouraging turtle-friendly beach practices.

The orange markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity along Indian River County’s 22.4-mile coastline. The county marks approximately one in 10 nests, and researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. Whalen said the long-term gains reflect years of work protecting sea turtles and their nesting beaches.

A nor’easter and king tides have brought powerful waves that strip sand from beaches, potentially exposing buried eggs. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween, though some nests may continue incubating beyond that date.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission says sea turtles spread their nests across the season, helping some survive even when storms damage others. After rough weather, beachgoers may encounter exposed eggs or young turtles washed ashore. FWC advises leaving exposed eggs in place rather than collecting or reburying them. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive.

Storm currents can also carry young turtles back ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. FWC says people should not pick them up or return them to the ocean. Instead, immediately call its 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance, according to FWC. Beachgoers can also help by removing beach gear, filling holes, flattening sandcastles and keeping lights off the beach at night.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Detective Horstman Released on $15,000 Bond in Felony DUI Case
hero.teaser: Detective Tyler Horstman was released Monday evening after posting $15,000 bond following his surrender on a felony DUI charge tied to an off-duty crash in Vero Beach.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Detective Tyler Horstman, who surrendered Monday on a felony DUI charge stemming from a March 2 off-duty crash in Vero Beach, was released Monday evening after posting $15,000 bond, according to Indian River County jail records. Horstman was driving a sheriff's office vehicle when the crash occurred, Sheriff Richard Del Toro Jr. said.

Horstman turned himself in at the Indian River County Jail on Monday afternoon, Oct. 26, after a felony arrest warrant was issued. Jail records list the charge as DUI causing serious bodily injury to another. Del Toro said the warrant involved an allegation of driving under the influence with a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury.

The Vero Beach Police Department led the criminal investigation into the March 2, 2026, crash. Del Toro said the sheriff's office learned Sept. 9 that blood testing indicated Horstman had a blood-alcohol concentration of 0.246. The sheriff said he immediately authorized an administrative investigation, and Horstman was placed on paid administrative leave Sept. 15.

After the felony warrant was issued and Horstman surrendered, he was placed on unpaid administrative leave under agency policy, Del Toro said. The sheriff's office has paused its internal investigation pending the outcome of the criminal proceedings. Vero Beach police remain the lead agency in the criminal case.

Del Toro said the allegations raise concerns for the community and the agency, which holds its personnel to high standards both on and off duty. The charge is an allegation, and Horstman's guilt or innocence has not been determined in court.

cards.headline: Siblings seek answers after St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge’s death
cards.teaser: Austin Hodge’s family says they were told he appeared normal before he was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk. His siblings are seeking answers about his final hours.
cards.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge are seeking answers about his death after being told the 34-year-old was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk early Saturday. Hodge died while on duty Oct. 24, just over a year after his younger brother, who also served with the fire district.

His sister, Alexis Hodge, said the family was told Austin had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis said the family wants to understand what happened in his final hours, including who was around him and who saw him before he was found unresponsive.

Alexis and her brother, Javan Hodge, gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. For Alexis, finding answers is part of moving forward: “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

The family is also grieving Jairus “Jay” Hodge, Austin’s 26-year-old brother. Family members said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. They said concerns about the medical care Jairus received led Austin to seek answers and advocate for his brother. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said. “He would not rest until he could spread Jay’s legacy globally.”

Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a healthcare career. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” he said. Alexis also said she intends to follow through on plans she shared with Austin. “I’m gonna do everything we talked about. And I’m gonna make him proud,” she said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective posts $15,000 bond in DUI case tied to Vero Beach crash
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Detective Tyler A. Horstman was released from jail Monday evening after posting $15,000 bond on a felony DUI charge stemming from a March 2 off-duty crash in Vero Beach, according to Indian River County jail records. He faces a charge of DUI causing serious bodily injury to another.

Horstman turned himself in to the Indian River County jail Monday afternoon, Oct. 26, the sheriff’s office said. The agency said it had been notified that a felony arrest warrant was issued alleging driving under the influence with a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or more and serious personal injury.

Horstman was operating a St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office vehicle when the crash occurred, according to the agency. The Vero Beach Police Department led the criminal investigation. The sheriff’s office said it was informed that Horstman’s blood test indicated a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246. Florida’s legal limit is 0.08.

After learning the blood test result, Sheriff Richard Del Toro Jr. immediately authorized an administrative investigation and placed Horstman on paid administrative leave, the sheriff’s office said.

“Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process,” the sheriff said in a statement Monday.

Tuesday’s approval came at the second reading, after commissioners advanced the moratorium Oct. 13. The pause comes as county leaders consider how to handle future data center development and residents raise concerns about the facilities’ future development.

cards.teaser: Both drivers were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce after the wrong-way collision at the Mall South Entrance intersection. Stuart police and the Florida Highway Patrol are investigating.
cards.body:
A 15-year-old driver and another motorist suffered serious injuries early Tuesday when a Stuart police pursuit ended in a wrong-way crash on U.S. Highway 1, according to the Stuart Police Department.

Officers were conducting traffic enforcement near Southwest Federal Highway and Southwest St. Lucie Crescent at about 3:45 a.m. when they spotted a vehicle traveling north at what they described as an extremely high rate of speed. An officer attempted a traffic stop, but the driver refused to stop and fled, police said.

The pursuit continued onto U.S. 1, where the driver began traveling north in the southbound lanes from Wright Boulevard, according to police. Officers continued trying to stop the vehicle because of the danger to other motorists. Police said officers also tried to alert drivers traveling on Northwest Federal Highway.

The fleeing vehicle collided with a southbound vehicle at the Mall South Entrance intersection, police said. Officers learned after the crash that the fleeing driver was 15 years old. Both drivers were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce with serious injuries.

The Stuart Police Department is investigating the incident. The Florida Highway Patrol is conducting a separate investigation into the crash.

cards.headline: King tides, strong winds flood Palm City; sheriff warns of further high water
cards.teaser: Floodwater off Dyer Point Road retreated Monday, but the sheriff’s office warned that high tide later that night could worsen conditions. Three high-water vehicles were ready for rescues.
cards.body:
Strong winds and king tides flooded parts of Palm City off Dyer Point Road on Monday, leaving some areas completely underwater. Although a resident said the water had retreated after several hours, the sheriff’s office warned that high tide later Monday night could make conditions worse and said three high-water vehicles were ready for rescues.

Terresa Baldwin, who lives off Dyer Point Road, said she also experienced flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals. Water rose over her dock and into her new patio. “The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that,” Baldwin said.

Baldwin described a sewage smell and dead copperheads in the floodwater. Even after the water went down, she remained concerned about flooding over the next few days. “The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see,” Baldwin said.

Lt. Dave Rosko urged residents to think twice before driving through floodwater and said people living in coastal communities should consider future tides before traveling. “Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters,” Rosko said. “If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety.”

hero.headline: Austin Hodge’s siblings seek answers after St. Lucie County firefighter’s death
hero.teaser: Alexis and Javan Hodge want to understand their brother’s final hours after he was found unresponsive at his firehouse. Their family lost another firefighter brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, in July 2025.
hero.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge are seeking answers about his final hours after the 34-year-old died on duty Oct. 24. His sister, Alexis Hodge, and brother, Javan Hodge, say they want to understand what happened before he was found unresponsive in his bunk at the firehouse early Saturday. Alexis said the family had been told he appeared to be himself in the hours before he was found unresponsive, cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis and Javan gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family.

The siblings said they want to learn who was around Austin and who saw him before he was found unresponsive. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. For Alexis, those answers are important to moving forward with her grief. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Austin’s death came just over a year after the death of his younger brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, 26, who also served with the fire district. The family said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. His medical care raised concerns for the family, and Austin sought answers and advocated for his brother, they said. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said.

Alexis and Javan said they are determined to carry on both brothers’ legacies. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a healthcare career. hero.headline: Martin County approves one-year data center pause; Kanner Highway proposal exempt
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted 4-0 Tuesday to approve a one-year moratorium on new data center development. An already-submitted proposal for a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway is exempt from the pause.

The county recently received the application for its first proposed data center in unincorporated Martin County, west of Interstate 95. Because the application was submitted before the moratorium, Tuesday's vote will not affect it.

The approval came on second reading after commissioners advanced the moratorium Oct. 13. The pause comes as county leaders consider how to handle future data center development and residents raise concerns about the facilities' future development.

cards.headline: Two drivers seriously injured in wrong-way U.S. Highway 1 crash after police pursuit
cards.teaser: A 15-year-old driver and another motorist were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce after the crash at the Mall South Entrance intersection. Stuart police and the Florida Highway Patrol are investigating.
cards.body:
A 15-year-old driver and another motorist were seriously injured early Tuesday after a police pursuit ended in a wrong-way crash on U.S. Highway 1, according to the Stuart Police Department.

Officers were conducting traffic enforcement near Southwest Federal Highway and Southwest St. Lucie Crescent at about 3:45 a.m. when they spotted a vehicle heading north at what they described as an extremely high rate of speed. An officer attempted a traffic stop, but the driver refused to stop and fled, police said.

The pursuit continued onto U.S. 1, where the driver began traveling north in the southbound lanes from Wright Boulevard, according to police. Officers continued trying to stop the vehicle because of the danger to other motorists and also attempted to alert drivers traveling on Northwest Federal Highway. The fleeing vehicle collided with a southbound vehicle at the Mall South Entrance intersection, police said.

Officers learned after the crash that the driver of the fleeing vehicle was 15 years old. Both drivers were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce with serious injuries. The Stuart Police Department is investigating the incident, and the Florida Highway Patrol is conducting a separate investigation into the crash.

cards.headline: Former Jensen Beach High School player Andrew Burnette gets another year at Louisiana Tech
cards.teaser: Burnette secured one more year of college football eligibility after a legal challenge against the NCAA, allowing him to return to Louisiana Tech.
cards.body:
Former Jensen Beach High School football player Andrew Burnette secured another year of college eligibility after a legal challenge against the NCAA, allowing him to return to Louisiana Tech. Burnette had exhausted his eligibility after his first season at the Division I level and spent a few months working with his father at a steel mill in Detroit before getting another chance to play.

This summer, the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, allowing student-athletes to compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. Burnette hired a lawyer and went to court against the NCAA to seek his final year of eligibility. He was granted one more year. “It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing,” said Burnette.

Burnette moved from Michigan around age 12 and played football in Martin County. He attended Jensen Beach High School originally for wrestling, then decided during high school that he wanted to pursue football. “I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan,” said Burnette.

Recruiting proved difficult. “One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited,” said Burnette. He went to Highland Community College in Kansas, where he played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns. He then transferred to Independence Junior College, where he was cut from the team.

Burnette next contacted Keiser University in West Palm Beach, which had offered him a chance to play while he was in high school. After reviewing his film, a coach invited him to join the program. In two years at Keiser, Burnette rushed for more than 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns, drawing interest from Division I programs, starting with Louisiana Tech.

“Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out,” said Burnette. His successful eligibility challenge has given him another season at Louisiana Tech.

hero.headline: Florida voters choose among Moody, Nixon and Gillespie in Senate special election
hero.body:
Early voting is underway in Florida’s special U.S. Senate election, with voters choosing among Republican incumbent Ashley Moody, Democratic challenger Angie Nixon and independent Neil Gillespie. Election Day is one week away. The winner will serve the final two years of Marco Rubio’s term. Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed Moody to the seat in January 2025 after Rubio left the Senate to become U.S. secretary of state.

Moody, a former two-term Florida attorney general from Plant City, has emphasized law enforcement and public safety, highlighting her experience as a federal prosecutor, judge and attorney general. At a recent campaign stop in Martin County with Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, she touted tax cuts enacted during President Donald Trump’s administration. Moody has described the election as a choice between “safety or chaos” and “freedom or socialism.”

Nixon, a state representative and labor organizer from Jacksonville, has centered her campaign on affordability and economic issues. She argues that working families are struggling with rising costs while politicians benefit from the current system. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America, Nixon supports a $25 minimum wage and Medicare for All and has campaigned alongside Bernie Sanders. She won a competitive Democratic primary against a more centrist opponent who significantly outraised her campaign.

Recent polling shows Moody leading by about four percentage points heading into the campaign’s final week. Florida last elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in 2012. Gillespie is also on the ballot as an independent candidate. The special election determines who will represent Florida for the remainder of Rubio’s term, with the seat returning to the ballot in 2028.

Martin County commissioners voted 4-0 Tuesday to approve a one-year moratorium on new data center development. A pending proposal for a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway is exempt because its application was submitted before the moratorium.

The proposed facility, west of Interstate 95, would be the first data center in unincorporated Martin County. The county recently received the application amid residents’ concerns about the future of data center development.

Tuesday’s approval came on the moratorium’s second reading, after commissioners moved it forward at their Oct. 13 meeting. The pause comes as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities.

hero.headline: Austin Hodge’s siblings seek answers after St. Lucie County firefighter’s death
hero.teaser: Alexis and Javan Hodge want to understand their brother’s final hours before he was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk Oct. 24.
hero.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge are seeking answers about his final hours after the 34-year-old was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk and died while on duty Oct. 24. Alexis Hodge and Javan Hodge say they want to understand what happened to their brother, whose death comes just over a year after they lost another brother who served with the fire district. Alexis said the family was told he had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. That account describes what relatives were told about his behavior before he was found unresponsive, rather than an explanation for his death.

Alexis and Javan gathered at Austin’s home, remembering him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family. “The feeling is unbearable,” Alexis said.

The siblings said their questions center on what happened before Austin was found unresponsive. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. Alexis said the family wants to identify who was around Austin and who saw him. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Their younger brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, was 26 when he died after becoming sick while on shift in July 2025, according to the family. Relatives said they had concerns about the medical care Jairus received and that Austin sought answers and advocated for him. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said.

Now, Alexis and Javan say they intend to carry on both brothers’ legacies. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue healthcare; he is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said.

hero.headline: Strong winds, king tides flood Palm City; sheriff’s office warns of more high water
hero.body:
Strong winds and king tides flooded parts of Palm City on Monday, leaving areas off Dyer Point Road underwater as the Martin County sheriff’s office warned that another high tide Monday night could worsen conditions. Three high-water vehicles were ready for rescue efforts, and residents were urged to avoid driving through flooded roads.

Dave Rosko said drivers should understand their vehicles’ limitations before entering high water. “Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters,” Rosko said. “If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety.” He also urged residents of coastal communities to be aware of future tides before traveling.

Terresa Baldwin, who lives off Dyer Point Road, said the area was flooded for a few hours before the water retreated. She also experienced flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals, with water covering her dock and reaching her new patio. “The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that,” Baldwin said.

Even as the water receded, Baldwin remained concerned about more flooding in the coming days. “The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see,” Baldwin said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective arrested on DUI charge after crash in agency vehicle
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Detective Tyler A. Horstman was arrested Monday, Oct. 26, on a charge of DUI causing serious bodily injury to another after an off-duty crash in Vero Beach while driving an agency vehicle. Horstman turned himself in to the Indian River County jail Monday afternoon, according to the sheriff’s office.

Indian River County jail records show Horstman was released Monday evening after posting $15,000 bond. The sheriff’s office said it was notified Monday that a felony arrest warrant had been issued for driving under the influence involving impairment, a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or more, and serious personal injury.

The crash occurred March 2 while Horstman was off duty and operating a St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office vehicle, according to the agency. The Vero Beach Police Department led the criminal investigation.

The sheriff’s office said it was informed that Horstman’s blood test indicated a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246. Florida’s blood alcohol limit is 0.08. After learning the test result, the sheriff immediately authorized an administrative investigation and placed Horstman on paid administrative leave, according to the agency.

“Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process,” the sheriff said in a statement Monday.

“The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires.”

cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie Police Department is asking for the public’s help finding Tatianna Ried, a 30-year-old woman who has been missing since mid-October.

Ried was last seen around noon on Oct. 17. Police are seeking information that could help locate her.

She is described as 5 feet 3 inches tall and weighing 170 pounds. She has black hair and brown eyes.

Anyone with information about the missing woman is asked to contact Detective J. Iannone at 772-807-4421 or email PSLMissingPersons@cityofpsl.com.

hero.headline: Strong winds, king tides flood Palm City as sheriff’s office warns of more high water
hero.body:
Strong winds and king tides flooded parts of Palm City off Dyer Point Road on Monday, and the Martin County sheriff’s office warned that high tide later Monday night could worsen conditions. Three high-water vehicles were ready for rescue efforts as officials urged residents to avoid driving through floodwater.

Dave Rosko said residents should understand their vehicles’ limitations before attempting to cross flooded areas. “Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters,” Rosko said. “If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety.” He also urged people living in coastal communities to consider future tides before traveling.

Terresa Baldwin, who lives off Dyer Point Road, said the roadway was flooded for a few hours before the water retreated. Parts of the area had been completely underwater. Baldwin said she smelled sewage and saw dead copperheads in the floodwater. She also experienced flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals, where water rose over her dock and into her new patio.

Although the water had receded, Baldwin remained concerned about flooding in the coming days, particularly overnight. “The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see,” Baldwin said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective arrested on DUI injury charge after Vero Beach crash
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Detective Tyler A. Horstman was arrested Monday, Oct. 26, on a charge of DUI causing serious bodily injury following an off-duty crash in Vero Beach. The sheriff’s office said Horstman turned himself in at the Indian River County jail Monday afternoon. Jail records list the charge as DUI causing serious bodily injury to another. He was released Monday evening after posting $15,000 bond. The arrest followed a criminal investigation led by the Vero Beach Police Department into the March 2 crash, which involved a vehicle belonging to the sheriff’s office.

According to the sheriff’s office, Horstman was off duty but driving an agency vehicle when the crash occurred. The agency said it was later informed that a blood test showed his blood alcohol concentration was 0.246. Florida’s legal blood alcohol limit is 0.08, putting the reported result at more than three times that limit. The blood test result was among the information the sheriff’s office disclosed in describing the case. Vero Beach police handled the criminal investigation, while the sheriff’s office separately initiated an administrative investigation concerning Horstman after learning of the test result.

The sheriff’s office said Sheriff Del Toro Jr. immediately authorized that administrative investigation and placed Horstman on paid administrative leave when the agency learned of the blood alcohol finding. Those actions came before Monday’s announcement about the felony arrest warrant. In its Monday account, the agency said it had been notified that a warrant had been issued for driving under the influence involving impairment, a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or more, and serious personal injury. Horstman’s surrender at the Indian River County jail and his release on bond both occurred later that day.

In a statement Monday, the sheriff’s office emphasized employees’ obligation to follow the laws they enforce and said accusations against an employee must be addressed through the appropriate process. “Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process,” the sheriff said. The statement also addressed the agency’s relationship with residents: “The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires.”

hero.headline: Fort Pierce procession honors St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge
hero.teaser: Monday’s funeral procession traveled from the Medical Examiner’s Office to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Loved ones remembered Hodge for his positive outlook and devotion to serving his community.
hero.body:
A funeral procession for St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died while on duty Oct. 24, left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Family and friends remembered him as a source of encouragement who loved serving his community and helped others pursue careers in firefighting.

Bernard Taylor knew Hodge since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior working as a counselor at the Boys and Girls Club when he met Hodge, a freshman he mentored. Hodge always wanted to keep up with the older kids, Taylor said, and their bond lasted for years. When Taylor later decided to change careers, Hodge was one of the first people he called. Hodge answered questions and helped Taylor with conditioning as he worked toward becoming a firefighter. “Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it,” Taylor said.

Taylor said he spoke with Hodge about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he was most heartbroken for Hodge’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Hodge’s mother, said she has been by her side. Hill said the family is relying on faith and a strong circle of support.

Hodge’s younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. Austin spent months searching for answers after his brother’s death and pushed state lawmakers to repeal Florida’s so-called free kill law. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, the law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin started a petition in his brother’s honor and said his fight was about accountability, not money. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin’s commitment to others: “He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community.”

A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

hero.headline: Flooding blocks SW Dyer Point Road in Palm City; deputies deploy high-water vehicles
hero.body:
King tide flooding made SW Dyer Point Road in Palm City impassable Monday, prompting Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies to bring in three high-water vehicles to help reach people stranded in vehicles or homes. The flooding came as a coastal flood warning remained in effect for coastal Martin County through 2 a.m. Thursday.

Flooding also was reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. One driver described water about waist-deep in part of the area. Resident Terresa Baldwin said water surrounded the front and back of her home and described Monday’s flooding as the worst she had seen in eight years. Baldwin also raised concerns about the water’s smell and said she believed it contained sewage rather than only runoff.

The National Weather Service’s coastal flood warning covers low-lying areas near the water in Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. The warning runs through 2 a.m. Thursday in coastal Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties and through 8 p.m. Wednesday in coastal Palm Beach County. More high tides were expected through Wednesday, with Monday’s high tide forecast for 9:06 p.m.

Deputies urged people to avoid flooded areas and not to drive through standing water. The sheriff’s office advised residents to call 911 if they need emergency assistance.

Flooding also was reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. One driver told CBS12 the water was about waist-deep in part of the area. Resident Terresa Baldwin said water came up around both the front and back of her home, and that Monday’s flooding was the worst she had seen in eight years. In Boynton Beach, flooding led to road closures, including at Ocean Avenue and Federal Highway. The Ocean Inlet Marina also closed because of high tides. In Boca Raton, water reached a Cub Scout pack’s campsite at Spanish River Park, prompting campers to move supplies to higher ground. Elsewhere, Midtown Beach was temporarily closed because of large surf and high tides. The northbound lane of South Ocean Boulevard between Chilean and Australian avenues was scheduled to close from 10 a.m. to noon while crews moved a lifeguard tower. hero.headline: Man arrested on loitering, prowling and trespassing charges in Hobe Sound
hero.teaser: Joseph Oswald, 28, was arrested after residents on Crooked Oak Avenue called 911 about suspicious activity, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.
hero.body:
Joseph Oswald, 28, was arrested on charges of loitering, prowling and trespassing after residents reported a disturbance in a Hobe Sound neighborhood, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

Residents along the 6000 block of Crooked Oak Avenue called 911 after Oswald was yelling at people and wandering through the neighborhood, deputies said. Responding deputies found Oswald, who appeared to be under the influence of an unknown substance, according to the sheriff's office.

The sheriff's office said Oswald had been released from prison 11 days before his arrest and had as many as 14 prior arrests in Martin County, on charges ranging from grand theft and burglary to loitering and prowling. The agency praised residents for quickly reporting the activity, saying community reports of suspicious behavior help keep neighborhoods safe.

Deputies responded and found Oswald, who appeared to be under the influence of an unknown substance, the sheriff's office said. See also: Woman with 28 prior felony convictions arrested in Okeechobee drug investigation Oswald has an extensive criminal history, with as many as 14 prior arrests in Martin County on charges ranging from grand theft and burglary to loitering and prowling, according to the sheriff's office. He now faces charges of loitering, prowling, and trespassing. The sheriff's office praised residents for quickly reporting the activity, saying community members play an important role in keeping their neighborhoods safe when they report suspicious behavior.

hero.headline: Coastal flood warning covers St. Lucie County through 2 a.m. Thursday
hero.body:
A coastal flood warning remains in effect for coastal St. Lucie County until 2 a.m. Thursday as king tides are expected to produce the season’s highest tides along Florida’s Atlantic coast. Low-lying locations close to the water are at risk of flooding, particularly where drainage is poor and around high tide. According to the National Weather Service, coastal Martin and Indian River counties are also under the warning until 2 a.m. Thursday. The warning for coastal Palm Beach County lasts until 8 p.m. Wednesday. Monday’s highest tide is expected at 9:06 p.m.

In Palm City, flooding has made SW Dyer Point Road impassable, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported. Flooding was also reported on SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. Images released by the Sheriff’s Office show widespread water across streets, with people walking through water reaching their ankles. The agency is sending high-water rescue vehicles to assist people stranded in homes or vehicles. Residents should stay away from the flooded area and call 911 if they need emergency help. Drivers should never attempt to cross a flooded road and should turn around instead. A separate video shows flooding on Indian River Drive, with a car traveling through the water.

In Boynton Beach, heavy flooding has closed the intersection of Ocean Avenue and Federal Highway. Drivers are being asked to stay clear of the intersection and take other routes. Officials plan to provide an update after the water drops and the intersection reopens. High tides have also forced the closure of Ocean Inlet Marina. Midtown Beach is temporarily closed because large surf and unusually high tides have made beach access unsafe, officials said. On South Ocean Boulevard, the northbound lane between Chilean Avenue and Australian Avenue will close from 10 a.m. to noon so crews can move a lifeguard tower.

Other coastal recreation areas are also affected. Delray Beach officials say red flags are flying at the city’s beach because of high surf and flooding. The Juno Beach Pier is closed until further notice after sustaining damage from a recent offshore surge and high surf. Those closures accompany the coastal flood warnings covering Palm Beach, Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties. With flooding more likely near high tide, residents in low-lying waterfront areas and places with poor drainage should avoid flooded roads. The safety message for motorists is to turn back rather than drive into floodwater.

cards.teaser: The proposed 120-pump travel center off Indrio Road and Interstate 95 still has county staff comments to address. Buc-ee's website lists a 2027 opening.
cards.body:
The proposed 120-pump Buc-ee's travel center off Indrio Road and Interstate 95 in St. Lucie County has received site plan approval, and its building permits are under review, county Planning Director Ben Balser said last week.

Responding to questions from a St. Lucie County commissioner, Balser said the county is ready to move forward once Buc-ee's addresses the remaining comments from county staff. Buc-ee's website continues to list the location as opening in 2027.

Plans for the travel center were first announced in 2023. The Texas-based chain is known for its large stores and expansive fueling areas. The St. Lucie County location would bring Buc-ee's to the Treasure Coast.

hero.headline: Man arrested after reported disturbance on Crooked Oak Avenue in Hobe Sound
hero.teaser: Joseph Oswald, 28, faces loitering, prowling and trespassing charges after residents called 911, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.
hero.body:
Joseph Oswald, 28, was arrested after residents along the 6000 block of Crooked Oak Avenue in Hobe Sound called 911 to report suspicious activity, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Deputies said he was yelling at people and wandering through the neighborhood.

Responding deputies found Oswald appearing to be under the influence of an unknown substance, the sheriff's office said. He faces charges of loitering, prowling and trespassing.

Oswald had been released from prison 11 days earlier. According to the sheriff's office, he has had as many as 14 prior arrests in Martin County on charges ranging from grand theft and burglary to loitering and prowling. The sheriff's office praised residents for quickly reporting the activity, saying community members play an important role in keeping their neighborhoods safe by reporting suspicious behavior.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge dies while on duty Oct. 24
hero.teaser: Austin Hodge served at Station 9 and had been with the district for more than nine years. The district will share memorial arrangements as they are finalized.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge died while on duty Saturday, Oct. 24, the St. Lucie County Fire District announced, calling his death a profound loss to the department and the fire service community. Hodge was assigned to Station 9 and had served the community for more than nine years after joining the district on July 17, 2017. Neighboring Indian River County Fire Rescue also shared condolences following his unexpected death Saturday morning. The circumstances surrounding his death have not been released.

Hodge’s death came more than a year after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic, died on July 22, 2025, at age 26. The brothers shared a close bond and a passion for serving their community. Austin had described Jarius as his best friend and said they enjoyed working alongside each other. He described his younger brother as someone who loved his family, his community and his country, loved going to work and pushed Austin to keep going.

Austin had said Jarius became ill after catching the flu from a patient at work in July 2025. According to Austin’s account, Jarius went to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie on July 22 because he was struggling to breathe and died hours later. Austin said his brother had been healthy before becoming ill. He alleged that medical staff made critical errors while treating Jarius, including taking three attempts to intubate him. Those claims were allegations Austin raised while seeking accountability for his brother’s death.

Austin also spoke publicly about Florida’s medical malpractice laws, arguing that restrictions on who can pursue certain wrongful-death claims prevented his family from seeking legal accountability. He emphasized that the family wanted the physicians held accountable rather than financial compensation. Following Austin’s death, the St. Lucie County Fire District asked the public to respect his family as they grieve. The district said information about memorial arrangements would be shared as details are finalized. It also said additional information about ways to honor his service would be shared in coordination with his family.

hero.headline: Donalds, Jolly outline differences on taxes, schools and data centers in Florida race
hero.body:
Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly outlined different approaches to property-tax revenue, school accountability and data centers in closing interviews as they campaigned across Florida. A University of North Florida poll released last week found the governor’s race statistically tied. Donalds, a Republican congressman, wants to build on the policies of outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis, while Jolly, who served in Congress as a Republican during the 2010s, is emphasizing housing, health care and education.

Donalds supports continuing Florida’s Department of Government Efficiency, which DeSantis created by executive order in 2025 and which has audited multiple counties. He said that work would be important if voters approve Amendment 3, which would raise homestead tax exemptions and reduce local revenue. Donalds said he has committed to a funding formula to help fiscally constrained counties whose budgets would change significantly. Jolly personally opposes the amendment but said he would support voters’ decision if it passes. “I think we all want the math behind Amendment 3 to work, but it just doesn't,” Jolly said.

Both candidates support keeping universal school vouchers. Jolly also wants greater transparency requirements for charter schools and higher pay for public school teachers. He said schools accepting vouchers should provide the same services, meet the same standards and face the same measures as public schools. Asked whether charter school financial records should be public, Donalds emphasized student achievement, including attainment in math and reading, along with ACT and SAT scores. “I think that's the accountability and the transparency that parents are looking for in the state of Florida, because at the end of the day, they're looking to make sure that the output is where it needs to be.”

The candidates also differ on data center construction. Jolly supports a moratorium, while Donalds said local governments should decide whether to allow the facilities. Donalds said that when local governments approve data centers, the state should protect water resources and ensure utility costs are not passed to consumers. Jolly said he wants to work across party lines on his broader agenda, arguing that expanding health care access would reduce costs and that investments in public education and stable housing would strengthen the economy. Donalds also pledged to continue immigration enforcement and expand government-efficiency reviews to local governments and state agencies throughout Florida.
hero.article_text: The race to be Florida's next governor is a competitive one — a statistical tie, according to a poll released last week by the University of North Florida.I caught up with Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Jolly as they each campaigned across the state, pitching different visions of Florida's future to voters.Donalds, a Republican congressman, told me in a video call from his campaign bus on the road that he wants to build on the policies he likes from Gov. Ron DeSantis' outgoing administration."We live in a great state, and what has separated us from the other states is we continue to choose common sense conservative policy," Donalds said.That includes immigration enforcement."We're going to continue that mission here in the great state of Florida because we are going to continue to follow the law. I think that's the appropriate use of state authority and state powers," Donalds said.It also includes Florida's Department of Government Efficiency, which DeSantis formed through an executive order in 2025 and has since conducted audits of multiple counties across Florida."We are going to DOGE all governments, both local and state agencies in the state of Florida, because it's not our tax money. It belongs to the people of Florida. We need to make sure that government lives within its means, the way families have to live within their means," Donalds said.Donalds told me that effort will be important if Amendment 3 passes, raising homestead tax exemptions and reducing local revenue. I asked him whether, as governor, he would be prepared if some of the municipalities that need help come to Tallahassee asking for it."Yes, we will, and we've already made a public commitment to the fiscally constrained counties in the state of Florida," Donalds said. "Those that we know that their budgets are going to change in a major way, that we're prepared to provide a funding formula for those fiscally constrained counties so that they can be able to make ends meet."Jolly, a Democrat who served as a Republican in Congress during the 2010s, visited WPTV as his campaign traveled through Palm Beach County. He has said he personally opposes Amendment 3, but will support the will of the voters if it passes."I think we all want the math behind Amendment 3 to work, but it just doesn't," Jolly said.Florida hasn't elected a Democrat as governor since the 1990s. I asked Jolly why he thinks that is and why he believes his campaign could overcome that."Look, we're a state that trended Republican, particularly in the last eight years, and we know by voter registration it's still a predominantly Republican state," Jolly said. "I think we're in a moment most akin to a 1974 post-Watergate moment, where voters are saying, 'Burn the ships. Let's go in a new direction.'"Jolly said that direction should be simple."Housing, healthcare, education, and no data centers. "The answers are not in ideology. The answers are in solutions."He also said he wants to reach across the aisle to achieve those goals."If we expand health care access, we reduce costs. So you can be a conservative that wants to save money or a progressive that wants more health care. When we invest in public education, we create a resilient economy that should be attractive to Republicans. The economic argument behind that, I think, on housing, when more people have stable housing, the economy is better. I think we can work with Republicans," Jolly said.One issue where the two candidates agree is on school choice. Both told me they support keeping universal vouchers in place.Jolly also emphasized his desire to increase transparency requirements in Florida's charter schools and increase teacher pay in public schools."Let's engage in a little bit of consumer protection here on behalf of kids and families, and say that if you're going to take a voucher as a school, you should have to provide the same services, standards and offerings and be measured by the same measuring stick that our public schools are," Jolly said.Asked whether financial records of charter schools should be public records, as they are for public schools, Donalds replied, "I think if you're talking about what parents are looking for, what they want to basically see, are the children being educated? What are the mathematical attainment scores of that school? What are the reading attainment scores of that school? And if you're talking about high school, what's the ACT scores and what's the SAT scores? I think that's the accountability and the transparency that parents are looking for in the state of Florida, because at the end of the day, they're looking to make sure that the output is where it needs to be."Donalds' wife, Erika Donalds, founded a charter school company and currently runs a nonprofit promoting school choice. "My wife is actually not in the charter school business anymore. She's actually been out of that business for a couple of years," Donalds told me. "But I just want to be clear: she will not be contracting with the state of Florida in any way, shape, or form."On data center policy, the candidates differ. Jolly said he supports a moratorium on data center construction, while Donalds believes those decisions should be left up to local governments."If a local government says no data centers, then no data centers. If they do, then where the state steps in is we make sure that utility bills, utility costs are not passed on to consumers, and we also make sure that we are going to protect water resources in our state," Donalds said.For the first time in decades, Florida voters did not get to see a gubernatorial debate for this election.Asked what he would say to Jolly had the two candidates faced one another on the debate stage, Donalds said, "I would like him to explain why and how the people of Florida are going to be able to pay for his insurance plan, because by independent analysis, his insurance plan will drive up premiums on the people of our state, and everybody will be hit with a $1,000 hurricane tax when the next time the big storm comes through," referring to the funding the sovereign wealth fund Jolly says he would like to create to cover windstorm damage for Florida homeowners. (Jolly has denied that the fund would impose a new tax.)"I'm not sure debates improve our politics at this point. I think they just platform the division and the vitriol and the ugliness," Jolly told me. "My wife says in a world of Donald Trump, I'm trying to be Ted Lasso. We have two young kids, and I want them to look back and know that Dad acted in a way that he spoke of, which was not to further devolve our politics into vitriol and ugliness and division. Debates are about who can score the greatest insult, and I just I don't think that helps."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, 34, dies on duty
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Fire District confirmed that firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, 34, died Saturday morning while on duty. Hodge joined the district on July 17, 2017, and was assigned to Station 9 in Fort Pierce.

A procession of firefighters and personnel from other agencies traveled from HCA Lawnwood Hospital to the morgue in Fort Pierce on Saturday morning. The district said it will share information about memorial arrangements and opportunities to honor Hodge’s service in coordination with his family as plans are finalized.

“His death is a profound loss to the St. Lucie County Fire District and the fire service community,” the agency said. “The District extends its heartfelt condolences to Hodge’s family, friends, and fellow firefighters during this difficult time.” The district also thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department, and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for supporting its firefighters and helping honor Hodge.

Hodge’s younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also served with the St. Lucie County Fire District. He died on July 22, 2025, after falling ill at work at Station 3. His family said he had the flu, felt weak and was later rushed to the hospital, where he died hours later. People gathered May 30 for a cookout and balloon release to celebrate what would have been his 27th birthday.

Austin Hodge spoke about his brother’s influence at that gathering. “He was a quiet leader, and we take a lot from him. He was my younger brother, but I looked up to him in many ways to keep me poised, keep me patient. And I think that's what he's teaching everybody today.”

Austin Hodge told WPBF at the time: "He was a quiet leader, and we take a lot from him. He was my younger brother, but I looked up to him in many ways to keep me poised, keep me patient. And I think that's what he's teaching everybody today." In June, another firefighter, Connor Whitehead, 21, died on May 31 but the cause of death wasn't released. Our hearts are with Austin’s family, loved ones, and everyone who had the privilege of serving alongside him. We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss." Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

hero.headline: Florida approves USAA auto insurance rate cuts averaging 7% for over 498,000 policies
hero.body:
Florida Insurance Commissioner Mike Yaworsky has approved USAA Group auto insurance rate reductions averaging 7% across more than 498,000 policies statewide, according to the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation. The approvals cover several auto insurance programs, with savings varying by program.

Average rate decreases range from 0.4% to 11.2%, according to the state. USAA has its highest concentration of Florida business in Brevard, Escambia and Okaloosa counties. Average reductions in those counties are 5.8% in Brevard, 8% in Escambia and 8.4% in Okaloosa.

“The Office of Insurance Regulation is constantly reaching out to insurers to inquire about rate relief, and USAA is always stepping up to the plate and looking out for their consumers,” Yaworsky said in a release. He also encouraged other insurers to consider additional rate reductions.

Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia characterized the reductions as another sign of improvement in the state's insurance market and credited Florida's tort reforms. “These auto insurance rate decreases will help Florida families keep more of their hard-earned money in their pockets, especially our military families,” Ingoglia said.

The latest approvals follow other savings USAA provided to Florida members over the past year. Between December 2025 and July 2026, the company provided nearly $1 billion in rate reductions and direct member returns, according to the release. That total included a $500 million dividend distributed to approximately 830,000 members.

State regulators also reported that Florida's five largest auto insurance groups have a combined indicated rate change of negative 12.6% for 2026. Those companies represent 81% of the state's auto insurance market, according to the release. The state also reported that Florida's personal auto liability loss ratio was 52.5% in 2025, the lowest in the nation and Florida's lowest level in 15 years.

Individual policyholders could see different savings depending on their program. According to the state, average rate changes range from a decrease of 0.4% to as much as 11.2%. USAA has its highest concentration of Florida business in Brevard, Escambia and Okaloosa counties. Average decreases in those counties are 5.8% in Brevard, 8% in Escambia and 8.4% in Okaloosa. 'The Office of Insurance Regulation is constantly reaching out to insurers to inquire about rate relief, and USAA is always stepping up to the plate and looking out for their consumers,' Yaworsky said in the release. He encouraged other insurers to consider additional rate reductions. Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia pointed to the reductions as another sign of improvement in the state's insurance market and credited Florida's tort reforms. 'These auto insurance rate decreases will help Florida families keep more of their hard-earned money in their pockets, especially our military families,' Ingoglia said. The latest reductions follow other savings announced by USAA over the past year. According to the release, the company provided nearly $1 billion in rate reductions and direct member returns to Florida members between December 2025 and July 2026. That included a $500 million dividend distributed to approximately 830,000 members. State regulators also said Florida's five largest auto insurance groups are showing a combined indicated rate change of negative 12.6% for 2026. Those companies represent 81% of Florida's auto insurance market, according to the release. The state also reported that Florida had the nation's lowest personal auto liability loss ratio in 2025 at 52.5%, its lowest level in 15 years.

hero.headline: Jensen Beach High School standout Andrew Burnette gains another year at Louisiana Tech
hero.body:
Former Jensen Beach High School standout Andrew Burnette has gained another season of football at Louisiana Tech after hiring a lawyer and challenging the NCAA over his eligibility. Burnette had exhausted his eligibility after his first season at the Division I level and spent a few months working with his father at a steel mill in Detroit. A change in NCAA eligibility rules this summer opened a path for him to seek one final year on the field.

Burnette moved from Michigan around age 12 and played football in Martin County. At Jensen Beach High School, wrestling initially drew him to the school. “I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion,” said Burnette. As he progressed through high school, his focus shifted toward football. He established himself on the football field but struggled to attract college recruiters. “One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited,” he said.

He began his college career at Highland Community College in Kansas, where he played nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns. He then transferred to Independence Junior College, where he was cut from the team. Burnette contacted Keiser University in West Palm Beach, which had offered him a chance to play while he was in high school. A coach reviewed his film and invited him to join the program. Over two years at Keiser, Burnette rushed for more than 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns, drawing interest from Division I programs, starting with Louisiana Tech.

After his first season at Louisiana Tech, Burnette returned to Michigan to work with his father. This summer, the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, allowing student-athletes to compete for up to five seasons within a continuous five-year period. Burnette hired a lawyer and went to court against the NCAA before receiving another year of eligibility. “It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing,” he said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, 34, dies while on duty
hero.body:
St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, 34, died Saturday morning while on duty, the St. Lucie County Fire District said. Hodge was assigned to Station 9 in Fort Pierce and had been with the district since July 17, 2017. Firefighters and personnel from other agencies took part in a procession Saturday morning from HCA Lawnwood Hospital to the morgue in Fort Pierce. The district described his death as a significant loss for its personnel and the broader fire service community. It offered condolences to his family, friends and fellow firefighters and said memorial arrangements would be announced as plans are completed with his family.

Hodge’s death came about a year after the death of his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, who also served with the St. Lucie County Fire District. Jarius died July 22, 2025, after becoming ill while working at Station 3. His family said he had the flu and felt weak before being rushed to a hospital, where he died hours later. On May 30, people gathered for a cookout and balloon release to mark what would have been his 27th birthday. Austin Hodge reflected on his brother’s influence at that gathering: “He was a quiet leader, and we take a lot from him. He was my younger brother, but I looked up to him in many ways to keep me poised, keep me patient. And I think that's what he's teaching everybody today.”

In the hours after Austin Hodge’s death, district firefighters, Honor Guard members and public safety partners gathered to honor him and support his family and colleagues. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties. It said their assistance helped ensure Hodge was treated with dignity and respect. The district also expressed gratitude to fellow first responders and community members for their support, describing the connections among firefighters as rooted in trust, shared experiences and commitment to one another.

Condolences also came from Port St. Lucie Fire Rescue, the Fort Pierce Police Officers Association, the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, Indian River County Emergency Services Department, Indian River County Fire Rescue, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue and Riviera Beach Fire Rescue. Another district firefighter, Connor Whitehead, 21, died May 31. The St. Lucie County Fire District has 20 fire stations and 523 firefighters, according to its website. It said information about opportunities to honor Austin Hodge’s service would be shared in coordination with his family as details are finalized.

cards.headline: Man dies after medical distress at Fort Pierce Service Plaza on Florida's Turnpike
cards.teaser: FHP said the man died at a hospital after being found unresponsive Sunday morning. Investigators do not suspect foul play.
cards.body:
A man who suffered medical distress Sunday morning at Fort Pierce Service Plaza on Florida's Turnpike died after being taken to a hospital, the Florida Highway Patrol said.

FHP units from Post 5 found the man at 5:40 a.m. He was unresponsive, was not breathing and had no pulse. He was transported to Florida Coast Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead, FHP said.

People traveling with the man said he had not been feeling well. FHP said no foul play is suspected in his death.

At 5:40 a.m., FHP units from Post 5 found an unresponsive man, who was not breathing and had no pulse. Lucie County Fire District spokesperson told WPBF the patient was transported to Florida Coast Medical Center in Port St. He was pronounced deceased at the hospital, FHP said. No foul play​ is suspected, as the people traveling with the person said he was not feeling well. hero.body:
Jensen Beach faced Fort Pierce Westwood on Friday with the District 13-4A football championship at stake, seeking its fourth district title in five years. The Falcons entered the matchup after a 51-0 victory over Legacy the previous week, a shutout highlighted by two defensive touchdowns from senior linebacker Alex Thornton. The district contest put Jensen Beach among the Treasure Coast teams playing for championship honors on a night that also brought a title-winning performance from Vero Beach. For the Falcons, the matchup with Westwood offered an opportunity to add another championship to their recent run of district success.

Thornton supplied two of the biggest plays in Jensen Beach’s win over Legacy, returning a pair of interceptions for touchdowns. His scoring returns were part of a performance in which the Falcons held their opponent scoreless while putting up 51 points. That result gave Jensen Beach momentum heading into its meeting with Fort Pierce Westwood, where the stakes shifted to the district championship. The Falcons’ pursuit of a fourth title in five years was a central storyline entering Friday’s game, following a week in which their defense contributed both points and a shutout.

Vero Beach secured the District 8-6A championship by defeating rival Treasure Coast 24-0 on Friday. The Fighting Indians’ defense kept Treasure Coast off the scoreboard, continuing its strong play late in the season. The victory stretched Vero Beach’s winning streak to six games and added a district championship to that run. Vero Beach had been pursuing a third straight district title, and the shutout against its rival continued the program’s sustained success in district competition. While Jensen Beach entered its matchup seeking another championship, Vero Beach delivered a title-clinching result with a three-touchdown margin and a clean defensive performance against Treasure Coast.

Elsewhere in the region, lightning affected the Friday schedule in Palm Beach County. Delays pushed back the start of play, but Dwyer and Royal Palm Beach eventually got underway. Benjamin was also in action at home, where its promising young players were among the featured performers. Those games formed part of a regional football night that included championship stakes, a rivalry shutout and weather interruptions. On the Treasure Coast, the district picture was the main focus: Vero Beach celebrated its District 8-6A title, while Jensen Beach’s meeting with Fort Pierce Westwood carried the District 13-4A championship stakes.

hero.headline: ACLU Letter Alleges Abuse, Medical Neglect at 'Deportation Depot' Facility
hero.body:
The ACLU and other advocacy groups have filed a letter alleging widespread abuse of detainees at the Florida immigration detention facility known as "Deportation Depot." The groups say they conducted dozens of interviews with people currently or recently detained at the facility, their loved ones, and attorneys who represent detainees there, and that those interviews point to a pattern of serious abuse.

The letter identifies seven categories of abuse: life-threatening medical neglect; lack of adequate food and clean drinking water; excessive, life-threatening heat; squalid, unsanitary, and unsafe living conditions; deprivation of necessities for physical, mental, and emotional wellbeing such as sleep, family visitation, and outdoor recreation; verbal and physical abuse and retaliation; and lack of access to the courts and to confidential communication with attorneys. On the issue of food, the letter states that detainees are not given enough nutritious food, describing portions as "extremely small, infant-sized food portions that are not filling" that lack adequate protein or nutrients. It cites cases of dramatic weight loss, including one detainee who lost 29 pounds in less than two months and another who lost 44 pounds over seven months.

On water, the letter alleges the facility does not provide adequate access to clean drinking water. It says the only water available in the dorms most of the time comes from visibly rusty fountains, and that newly arrived detainees are warned by others not to drink from them because many people have gotten sick doing so. One former detainee named Ryan said he and others would try to drink as much water as possible from the cafeteria during their brief mealtimes because it was the only source of clean water. He said that in the dorms, "you had no alternative sometimes than just to kind of take your chances with the water," describing it as having "a very strong metallic taste" that made his stomach feel like "something was kicking and punching" it once it settled.

ACLU attorney Amy Godshall, who wrote the letter, said the facility appears designed to strip detainees of basic dignity. "It's very much a cruel facility that's designed to deny people every aspect of humanity and decency and dignity, and is designed to make people physically weak, mentally weak, and just pressured to agree to the point where they agree to self deportation," she said. The letter argues this pressure may be intentional, stating there is evidence of a deliberate effort to make detention conditions unbearable so that people give up their legal rights and accept removal, adding that whether or not the conditions are intentional, they are punitive and unconstitutional. Ryan said he was approached by guards on three or four separate occasions and asked to sign forms consenting to his own deportation. "The question that a lot of us had is, well, if we were deportable, then why would we have to sign this document to make us deportable?" he said.

When Alligator Alcatraz shut down over the summer, it didn't end Florida's involvement in immigration detention. There's a second state-run facility that's been open for a year in a former prison about 50 minutes west of Jacksonville. Because its location is less controversial than the Everglades, it's flown largely under the radar. But now, detainees are speaking up about the alleged horrors inside what state officials have dubbed 'Deportation Depot.' 'It's insane. There's no other word [to describe the situation] than insanity. Just how bad these conditions were,' said a man who asked that we hide his face and refer to him by his middle name, Ryan. He fears being publicly identified could jeopardize his still-pending immigration case. 'I'm happy to be here, and I'm grateful, and obviously I'm gonna do everything I can to complete my immigration journey, and hopefully I can put this behind me,' Ryan said. I learned from the American Civil Liberties Union and confirmed through federal court records and local news reports that Ryan was detained by immigration authorities in late February and sent to the Baker Correctional Institution in Sanderson, where he spent four months. According to the most recent ICE detention data from July, roughly a thousand migrant men are housed at Baker. The ACLU put the number even higher, at about 1,200, during Ryan's stay. 'They were businessmen, entrepreneurs, paramedics, people that had been in the military. It was just, it was just everyone,' Ryan said. Ryan told me about 100 people in his dorm, with four working toilets and four working showers. He described the bathrooms as filthy, toiletries as scarce, and extreme heat as a persistent problem. 'We had one small AC unit in the corner of the room, which didn't work because the windows were smashed open anyway and kind of had been left broken,' Ryan said. 'We had black mold, brown mold. Like I said, those infestations of creatures. We had spiders, fire ants, cockroaches, bugs of all description.'
